title: Sovereign Liability Management

detail.title: Sovereign Liability Management
detail.abstract: Sovereign debt restructurings have long been criticized as slow, disorderly, and value-destructive. This has prompted recurring calls for a centralized and institutionalized statutory scheme to resolve sovereign debts modeled on Chapter 11 bankruptcy law. These proposals misunderstand how sovereigns have historically restructured their debts and the current state of corporate debt restructuring itself. Sovereigns have effectively restructured their debts through an ad-hoc and agile combination of domestic legislation, foreign policy, and contractual mechanisms. Meanwhile, corporates themselves have increasingly turned away from statutory proceedings in favor of out-of-court liability management exercises (LMEs)-transactions that use contractual flexibility to deliver new liquidity, discount capture, extended maturities, and reduced interest expense for the debtor and, in the process, create new creditor priorities in the restructured capital structure. The convergence between sovereign and corporate debt restructuring has therefore moved in an unexpected direction: corporates have converged toward the ad-hoc and contractual approach favored by sovereigns faster than sovereigns have converged toward the institutionalized and statutory approach available to corporates. This paper argues that the moment is ripe for sovereigns to complete the convergence by adopting the LME playbook. Sovereign LMEs would complement existing restructuring tools, unlock the full value of sovereign debt contracts, enable restructuring value creation through creditor differentiation, and advance the growing norm of proactive sovereign debt management through market-based transactions. Instead of a departure from sovereign debt restructuring traditions and practices, LMEs represent their fullest and most modern realization.

title: Copyright and Artificial Intelligence: The Importance of Memorisation and Attribution

detail.title: Copyright and Artificial Intelligence: The Importance of Memorisation and Attribution
detail.abstract: The intersection of copyright law and artificial intelligence raises fundamental questions about the optimal scope and form of intellectual property protection in a world of generative AI. Drawing on the economics of information goods, the technical literature on memorisation in large language models, and a comparative analysis of recent legal developments across Germany, the United Kingdom and the United States, this paper distinguishes two markets in which AI and copyright interact – the market for training data access and the market for reproduced outputs – and shows that they raise distinct welfare problems. Building on Gans (2024), we propose a capability-based levy that links payments to rights holders to the measurable memorisation rate of deployed models to reflect the potential harm caused in the market for reproduced outputs. We argue that the distribution problem that any such mechanism creates, as well as the non-pecuniary harm to creators from unattributed use of their work, can be addressed by mandating source-attribution capability at the model-architecture level. The capability-based approach has implementation advantages over training-data-based schemes, including reduced exposure to territorial arbitrage and stronger incentives for AI developers to reduce memorisation.

title: Organizational Structural Deviation: An Analytical Formulation for Measuring Structural Coherence in Strategic Decisions

detail.abstract:
Every strategic decision is only as strong as the reading that precedes it. Organizational diagnosis has been based predominantly on perception — assessments conducted by those who live within the system they intend to read. This approach presents a structural limitation: it does not allow measurement of the gap between what an organization intends to execute and what its internal architecture can effectively absorb.
This paper presents the Organizational Structural Deviation Model — a formal analytical formulation that measures, ex ante and based on observable evidence, the coherence between a declared strategic intention and the organization's structural capacity to execute it.
The model formalizes three core constructs: Decision Intensity (DI), which parameterizes the structural demand imposed by a strategic decision; Structural Coherence (SC), which quantifies the organization's integrated systemic capacity across four interdependent dimensions; and Structural Deviation (SD), which expresses the pressure resulting from the imbalance between DI and SC. From these constructs, the model derives a structural regime classification that translates the quantitative result into governance-oriented implications.
In contrast to existing approaches — predominantly retrospective, segmented by domain, or perception-based — the model operates at a moment prior to strategic commitment, grounded in documentable evidence, producing auditable and reproducible results.

The model emerges from the systematic formalization of patterns observed over more than two decades of structural analysis in B2B organizations facing strategic decisions. It addresses a recurrent gap in the literature: the absence of a parametric instrument capable of measuring, before execution, the organization's structural capacity to absorb the decision.

title: The Market for Oversight: Why Boards Stop Seeing Reality
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Market for Oversight: Why Boards Stop Seeing Reality
detail.abstract: Modern boards do not always fail because they lack information. More often, they fail because they see corporate risk through instruments that convert operating reality into reviewable, defensible, and administratively usable forms. This paper develops the concept of the market for oversight: the institutional supply chain through which management, advisers, auditors, consultants, lawyers, compliance personnel, and reporting systems produce board-facing representations of corporate risk. Although these artifacts are indispensable to governance, they may also become substitutes for reality testing. Drawing on corporate governance doctrine, board information asymmetry, risk governance, internal controls, organizational decoupling, and expert-mediated governance, the paper argues that the market for oversight can generate defensible abstraction: documented evidence of review, discussion, delegation, and monitoring that does not necessarily establish that the underlying risk is understood or controlled. The paper offers a mechanism-centered account of how board oversight can deteriorate despite visible process, expert validation, and formal reporting systems. Its central claim is that governance may become more documentable precisely as its contact with operating reality becomes weaker.

detail.abstract: Does military involvement in domestic emergency response improve citizens' perception of the armed forces? This paper examines this question using Spain's Emergency Military Unit (UME) as a case study. By combining provincial-level information on cumulative UME interventions with public opinion survey data from the Center for Sociological Research, I compare individuals with varying degrees of exposure to UME interventions, both across provinces and over time, taking into account the nonrandom distribution of interventions. I find robust evidence of a positive effect of exposure to UME interventions on perception of the Spanish armed forces. Preliminary research exploring media coverage and news exposure as key underlying mechanisms is also presented.

title: The Value of Class-Action Waivers: Evidence from Invalidation of the CFPB Arbitration Rule
affiliations: Chicago-Kent College of Law - Illinois Institute of Technology

detail.title: The Value of Class-Action Waivers: Evidence from Invalidation of the CFPB Arbitration Rule
detail.abstract: Do investors price the protection that mandatory arbitration clauses provide against class-action litigation? This paper answers that question by conducting an event study around eleven regulatory and legislative events—spanning the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's arbitration study, its proposed and final rule, and Congress's 2017 repeal—that shifted the likelihood that class-action waivers would remain enforceable in consumer financial contracts. We compare cumulative abnormal returns (CARs) for 47 publicly traded consumer financial services firms over 2012-2017 using a 250-day estimation window and ±2 trading-day event windows, estimated under both the standard market model and the Fama-French four-factor model. Treated firms subject to the CFPB rule moved in the predicted direction significantly more than control firms (comparable financial-services firms without product lines subject to the rule): the Fama-French treated coefficient is +0.71% per event (p < 0.001). The Senate's approval of the Congressional Review Act resolution is the strongest single signal, with a treated-control CAR differential of +2.22% (market model, p < 0.01) and +1.92% (FF, p < 0.05). Direction consistency across events is 6/11 under the market model and 8/11 under the FF model. Panel regressions controlling for market beta, event fixed effects, and sector confirm the main result; the FF specification is robust to excluding the dominant event, winsorizing, and dropping a potentially contaminated control firm. These findings are consistent with investors pricing arbitration protection as a meaningful source of firm value.

detail.abstract:
This Annex documents the canonicalisation methodology and variance decomposition framework developed for the Meridian Autonomy™ substrate underpinning Collins (2026e), The Stationary Sea Part 1. It is a companion to that paper rather than a revision of it. The Annex is published separately for two reasons. First, traceability: the substrate work documented in Part 1 was sealed at the v13.1.0 founding cohort 29 April 2026, and the canonicalisation framework was developed subsequently. Reporting the framework as an annex preserves the seal on the founding cohort while disclosing the methodological extension. Second, honesty: the framework is in active development with acknowledged limitations and blind spots that are not yet resolved. Folding it silently into Part 1 would obscure that development state. The Annex makes the development sequence and its limitations explicit.

The Annex contributes four methodological elements. First, a foundational principle distinguishing destructive variance (instrument-induced) from institutional signal (genuine change). Second, a two-lane canonicalisation framework partitioning the canonicalisation problem along the temporal axis: Lane 1 within-snapshot strict canonicalisation, Lane 2 cross-cycle bridging classifier. Third, a variance decomposition framework attributing observed variance to four components: A retrieval, B model, C code, D institutional. Fourth, integration with the Empirical Prediction Architecture (Stationary Sea Part 1 Section 7) extending pre-registration discipline to canonicalisation outcomes.

The Annex also discloses seven acknowledged limitations of the framework as of the writing date. These limitations are documented as a substantive section of the paper, in the spirit of the methodology lineage that prioritises explicit disclosure of unknowns over silent compromise. The limitations are operationally significant: they constrain the claims the framework can support at this iteration, and they motivate the next round of work.
This Annex does not revise any empirical finding reported in Part 1. The v13.1.0 founding cohort substrate, the architectural envelope predictions confirmed at sealing, and the cross-version recovery analysis between v11.1 and v13.1.0 stand as documented in Part 1. The Annex extends the methodology, not the substrate. The empirical findings of the variance attribution pilot fired 11 May 2026 to 12 May 2026 across four institutions in three regulatory regimes are reported in Stationary Sea Part 2, the companion empirical paper, which cites this Annex as the methodology source-of-truth for the two-lane framework and the four-component decomposition.

title: Balancing Speed and Reliability: Examining Consumer Perceptions in Quick Commerce Platforms in the Indian Context

detail.title: Balancing Speed and Reliability: Examining Consumer Perceptions in Quick Commerce Platforms in the Indian Context
detail.abstract: The rapid growth of quick commerce (q-commerce) has transformed the retail landscape by prioritizing ultra-fast delivery and convenience. While speed has emerged as a key differentiator, concerns regarding service reliability continue to influence consumer perceptions and long-term engagement. This study critically reviews existing literature to examine the trade-off between delivery speed and reliability in shaping consumer satisfaction, and bonding within the Indian qcommerce environment. Deploying marketing theories, including the Technology Acceptance Model and quality service, the paper is based on recent empirical and conceptual studies risk stressing the growing importance of reliability in sustaining customer relationships. The findings suggest that although speed drives initial adoption, reliability plays a more significant role in fostering trust and repeat usage. The overall aim of the study is to the support the budding concept and scenario of q-commerce by integrating marketing and operational perspectives and identifying critical research gaps for future empirical endeavors.

title: Beyond Themed Schools: Educational Architecture, Developmental Ecosystems, and Longitudinal District Coherence in Richmond Public Schools

detail.title: Beyond Themed Schools: Educational Architecture, Developmental Ecosystems, and Longitudinal District Coherence in Richmond Public Schools
detail.abstract:
Urban school districts across the United States continue adopting themed schools, magnet programs, specialty academies, and differentiated institutional models in attempts to improve engagement, strengthen workforce readiness, increase enrollment, and modernize secondary education systems. Richmond Public Schools (RPS) represents an especially significant case study because the district has repeatedly experimented with differentiated school identities and specialized educational structures for more than a century, including business-oriented education, vocational and industrial pathways, military structures, selective academic programs, arts centered programming, and specialized admissions schools. 

This paper argues that Richmond should avoid repeating historical cycles of large-scale thematic school differentiation and instead pursue a districtwide Comprehensive Developmental Ecosystem Model grounded in the field of Educational Architecture. Using a conceptual policy and systems analysis methodology, the paper examines how themed schools and differentiated institutional identities influence district coherence, public perception, enrollment behavior, transportation equity, developmental stability, and opportunity access.

title: A Comparative Study of Human Life Time Utilization

detail.title: A Comparative Study of Human Life Time Utilization
detail.abstract: Human life is a finite cycle in which individuals continuously attempt to balance daily necessities, social responsibilities, mental activities, and rest. Generally, people assume that they have sufficient time throughout life; however, a comprehensive analysis of daily activities reveals that the amount of truly productive and conscious time is comparatively limited. This research paper presents a comparative study of time utilization in an average 70-year human lifespan by analysing various daily activities such as sleep, bathing, eating, commuting, restroom usage, social activities, mobile phone usage, stress, waiting, traffic delays, and mental distractions. The study demonstrates that a significant portion of human life is consumed by routine activities and unproductive engagements, leaving only a limited duration for meaningful, conscious, and productive living. The study provides an important scientific and philosophical foundation for understanding time management, quality of life, self-awareness, and human consciousness.

title: The Umarell Effect: Assessing the Impact of Informal Public Oversight on Safety Compliance, Operational Integrity, and the Survivability of Indigenous Construction SMEs
affiliations: University of Nigeria

detail.title: The Umarell Effect: Assessing the Impact of Informal Public Oversight on Safety Compliance, Operational Integrity, and the Survivability of Indigenous Construction SMEs
detail.abstract: This paper examines how informal public oversight, drawing from the Italian cultural phenomenon of the "Umarell" (retired men who observe construction sites), intersects with established psychological frameworks such as the Hawthorne Effect, and how this intersection can be leveraged as a stakeholder management strategy for Indigenous construction small and medium enterprises (SMEs). The Umarell, once regarded as a figure of gentle amusement in Bolognese street culture, has gained institutional recognition as a legitimate site monitor, with the municipality of Riccione allocating public funds to formalize this role. This paper synthesizes literature from construction safety, Indigenous knowledge systems, SME survivability, and social license to operate in order to propose a unified theoretical framework called "The Umarell Effect," which positions informal public oversight as a strategic asset for construction project management and SME sustainability. Key findings from the literature review indicate that informal oversight mechanisms can reduce material theft by up to 24 percent, that the Hawthorne Effect demonstrates observable behavioral improvements under observation even in the absence of regulatory pressure, and that Indigenous Elders serve a parallel function as cultural guardians whose presence enhances safety compliance and operational integrity on construction sites. The paper argues that these phenomena share a common psychological and social mechanism: the sustained presence of community observers modifies worker behavior, deters fraud, and strengthens stakeholder trust. The proposed theoretical framework identifies three dimensions of the Umarell Effect, namely the behavioral, governance, and cultural dimensions, and discusses how each operates independently while reinforcing the others. The paper concludes with practical implications for Indigenous construction SMEs, identifies limitations of the existing literature, and proposes directions for future empirical research.

detail.abstract: Although radicalization in Pakistan has been widely studied, there is little understanding of how institutions keep supporting norms that encourage extremism. This article introduces the idea of the institutional echo chamber, showing how selection processes, control of information, and social pressures in schools, especially madrassas and universities, work together to limit different viewpoints, reduce contact both between and within faith groups, and encourage conformity. These institutional factors are different from individual paths to radicalization. Using evidence from two major Preventing and Countering Violent Extremism (P/CVE) programs in Pakistan, the Salamti Fellowship (390 fellows, 13 groups, 2018-2025, across 49 districts) and the Peace, Advocacy and Community Engagement through Transformation (PACT) for Tolerance program (66 universities, 85 vice chancellor meetings, 18 focus groups, 2019-2023), the article creates a two-level analysis. The first level uses contact theory to understand changes in individuals and their networks, with the Salamti Fellowship showing that ongoing, structured, residential contact can break echo chamber effects at the individual level. The second level shows how the structure of Pakistan's universities limits these individual changes, leading to what is called bounded disruption. The PACT program also shows nominal reform, with leadership-level promises not matched by real changes at the individual and network levels. The findings show that lasting P/CVE impact requires work at both levels, as efforts at only one level are insufficient. The article concludes by proposing a two-level intervention plan and calling for further research on these processes.

detail.abstract:
This paper reports a four-institution empirical validation of substrate identification reproducibility for the Meridian Autonomy™ substrate (Collins, 2026e), built on the two-lane canonicalisation framework and four-component variance decomposition of Annex 1a v1.0 (Collins, 2026i).

A pre-registered variance attribution pilot was fired on 11 May 2026 across four institutions and 13 cycles. The pre-registered raw agent-name Jaccard prediction of 0.90 falsified at an observed mean of 0.162, the pre-registered halt below 0.30 was honoured, and three substrate-level instruments (bridge rate, fragmentation collapse, cumulative cross-cycle coverage) were established as the correct measurement layer. Combined bridge rate across all 13 cycles was 56.50 percent. Fragmentation factor collapsed universally to a 1.331 to 1.744 band.

Two architectural commitments follow. First, a hundreds-not-thousands counter-prior: institution-level agent counts cluster in the 100 to 300 range, with no institution crossing 1,000 across nine months of operation, four scanner versions, two hardware platforms, and three classifier prompt variants. Second, a cross-institutional heterogeneity finding that refutes an earlier downward-offset reading; observed c_gov offsets against the April baseline range from minus 10.54 percent to plus 25.12 percent, the upward case being composition-driven. Heterogeneity is the headline finding.

The paper proposes that canonicalisation metrics may operate as an external instrument for disclosure coherence. A six-institution deterministic-mode panel partitions cleanly into high-bridge low-fragmentation and low-bridge high-fragmentation clusters, with no cycle crossing the boundary across 24 wet cycles. The hypothesis is reported as worth study at population scale and operationalisation is deferred. Appendix A maps the infrastructure to DORA, the EU AI Act, and ISO 27001.

detail.abstract:
AI agents are reshaping knowledge work, but the productivity gains are profoundly uneven. In a 2025 randomized trial of experienced developers, AI use was associated with a 19% slowdown-and the developers reported feeling faster the entire time. 1 Other 2023-2025 randomized trials, in management consulting, 2 customer service, 3 and law, 4 find large positive effects on bounded, well-specified work. MIT's NANDA initiative finds that 95% of corporate generative-AI pilots stall outright. 5 The variance is the point, and it does not track tool access. 
The operative production unit has changed: not the labor-plus-capital primitive of economics textbooks, which IDEs and spreadsheets already changed, but the smallest organizational element around which work is planned, staffed, billed, and managed. The new unit is the knowledge worker plus their orchestrated agents (the orchestrator-hour), and it absorbs functions that previously lived in three separate roles. Almost every system built around the old unit is now mispriced: hiring filters, billing rates, sprint cadence, the cultural ideal of deep work, and what organizations celebrate in their best people.
Three connected shifts are required to capture the upside. Individuals must learn to orchestrate parallel agent workstreams rather than execute serially. Work must be restructured around judgment density rather than execution throughput. And the deep-work cultural orthodoxy must give way to a more honest two-mode pattern of agent-in-the-loop work — broad supervision of several streams in parallel, and close foreground co-creation with one agent at close watch — both replacing solo composition as the default for serious technical work. Organizations that restructure deliberately will compound a margin and talent advantage that is difficult to copy after the fact.

detail.abstract:
The global expansion of Artificial Intelligence in educational settings has outpaced the development of institutional governance mechanisms to ensure its safe and ethical deployment. While regulatory frameworks such as the EU AI Act and India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 address national-level obligations, a critical implementation gap persists at the institutional level — within the schools, colleges, and EdTech platforms where AI systems are actively deployed. This paper introduces the concept of the Institutional Compliance Layer — a structured, school-embedded governance architecture that bridges national regulation and classroom practice.
Drawing on empirical evidence from a first-of-its-kind compliance audit of an AI platform deployed across Indian K-12 schools, and framed against the UNESCO Global Education Monitoring Report 2023 finding that only 1 in 7 countries legally guarantee the privacy of educational data (UNESCO, 2023), we argue that institutional compliance frameworks are not a supplementary consideration but a structural prerequisite for responsible EdTech deployment. We present the TAMIZH-G Framework — a Transparent, Accountable, MandateDriven, Integrity-Based, Zero-Bias, Human-Centric Governance model — as a replicable, South Asian model of institutional AI governance. We further propose a comparative lens on European developments, with particular reference to frameworks aimed at democratizing AI and empowering citizens through transparency.

title: Dual-use Risks of Frontier Artificial Intelligence

detail.title: Dual-use Risks of Frontier Artificial Intelligence

detail.abstract:
Background. The dual-use risks of frontier artificial intelligence systems have moved from prospective concern to operational reality. Anthropic's activation of AI Safety Level 3 safeguards for Claude Opus 4 in May 2025, explicitly because chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) uplift risks could no longer be confidently ruled out, marked a watershed in the industry's acknowledgement of risk. The United Kingdom AI Security Institute's first public Frontier Trends Report documented frontier model performance on apprentice-level cyber tasks rising from sub-nine per cent in late 2023 to approximately fifty per cent by 2026, with the first model completing expert-level tasks in 2025. The regulatory architecture intended to manage these risks remains unsettled: the United States Bureau of Industry and Security issued a Framework for Artificial Intelligence Diffusion in January 2025 and rescinded it in May 2025, leaving a regulatory gap that subsequent guidance has only partially filled.

Purpose. This paper provides a synthesis of dual-use risk evidence for frontier AI across cyber offensive uplift and CBRN uplift, maps the contemporary regulatory architecture including its current volatility, examines the diversion and weight-exfiltration risks that connect dual-use concerns to AI supply chain governance, and analyses the Gulf Cooperation Council strategic context where the United Arab Emirates and the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia occupy a distinctive position in global AI diffusion policy.

Approach. The paper adopts a narrative review methodology combining contemporary 2024 to 2026 empirical evaluations of frontier AI capabilities (including the UK AI Security Institute trends report, Anthropic Frontier Red Team disclosures, Frontier Model Forum threshold work, and independent third-party assessments), primary regulatory document analysis (the BIS Framework for AI Diffusion and its rescission, the EU AI Act systemic risk provisions, EU Regulation 2021 slash 821 on dual-use exports, the UAE Strategic Goods regime under Cabinet Resolution 50 of 2020), and analysis of voluntary industry safety frameworks (the Anthropic Responsible Scaling Policy, Google DeepMind Frontier Safety Framework version 2.0, OpenAI Preparedness Framework, and parallel instruments from Microsoft, Amazon, and G42).

Findings. Three findings emerge. First, the empirical evidence base for cyber offensive uplift is now substantial, with multiple converging signals indicating that frontier models provide meaningful tactical uplift to human cyber operators, particularly when paired with appropriate scaffolding; the evidence base for CBRN uplift is more contested due to sensitivity restrictions on full evaluation data, but is sufficient to support the precautionary safeguards that leading labs have implemented. Second, the regulatory architecture is in active flux: the AI Diffusion Rule episode illustrates that unilateral commodity-based export controls struggle with a technology that diffuses through training compute, weights distribution, and inference access in ways that traditional dual-use frameworks were not designed to capture. Third, the GCC strategic context is distinctive: the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia are positioned as Tier 2 destinations in US export-control thinking, with the UAE in particular having demonstrated a willingness to accommodate US security concerns through G42's divestment of Chinese hardware and the March 2025 US-UAE 1.4 trillion technology investment framework.

Implications. Practitioners deploying frontier AI in the GCC region operate under a multi-layered governance regime that combines formal export controls, voluntary industry safety frameworks, and emerging EU AI Act systemic risk obligations. The diversion risks examined in Section 5 connect directly to the AI Supply Chain Trust Boundary Model developed in Paper 10 of this slate, with weight exfiltration at Layer 2 representing the operational manifestation of the most consequential dual-use diversion concern. Future work will extend the analysis through comparative regulatory mapping (Paper 14) and operational identity considerations, including weight-level attestation (Paper 15).

title: A Systematization of Knowledge on DeFi Vaults: Architectures, Curation Mechanisms, and Strategy Design

detail.abstract:
Decentralized finance (DeFi) vaults are smart-contract-based asset management systems that pool deposits, execute programmable strategies, and mint tokenized shares representing claims on underlying assets and strategy performance. As vault designs have evolved from early yield aggregators to modular, actively managed systems, a new control layer, curation, has emerged to select strategies, configure risk parameters, and coordinate operational execution, introducing principal-agent dynamics and new failure modes. 

This paper systematizes DeFi vault architectures and curator-mediated control planes through (i) a unified system model and formal definitions for share accounting, roles, and operational dependencies, and (ii) three complementary taxonomies covering vault exposures and objectives, curator governance and accountability mechanisms, and strategy execution patterns together with their failure modes. We further map a representative set of production protocols to the proposed dimensions. The frameworks in this work aim to support rigorous analysis and safer design of blockchain-based financial applications.

title: Information Systems Security Policy Recommendation for Establishing a Framework for Security & Control and Technologies & Tools for Protecting Information Resources
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Information Systems Security Policy Recommendation for Establishing a Framework for Security & Control and Technologies & Tools for Protecting Information Resources
detail.abstract: This policy recommendation outlines a phased, right-sized framework for information systems security tailored to small businesses handling sensitive academic records, exemplified by K&K Print Supply and Services. Operating with limited ICT resources and budget, K&K faces vulnerabilities such as shared accounts, lack of backups, and reliance on basic antivirus tools. Drawing from Laudon & Laudon (2022) and Abante, Lacorte, & Gongora (2023), the framework emphasizes affordable, scalable controls—formal policies, individual user accounts, UPS units, and bundled security suites—aligned with the Philippine Data Privacy Act of 2012 and GDPR standards. The proposed three-stage implementation (Foundation, Core Implementation, Expansion) ensures sustainability, compliance, and trust by progressively integrating encryption, backup systems, identity management, and secure networking. This incremental approach demonstrates that small businesses can achieve credible information security without excessive costs, fostering operational continuity and stakeholder confidence through documented governance and deliberate investment.

Enterprise systems have reached a structural inflection point. Organisations now generate more data,
deploy more analytical tools, and operate with more interconnected processes than at any prior
moment — yet persistently fail to translate computational capability into decision quality, traceability,
or institutional learning. The root cause is architectural: enterprise systems are designed to record
and execute transactions, not to reason about decisions and compound knowledge over time. This
paper establishes the foundational architecture of Decision-Making Driven Design (DMDD) — a
design science framework that repositions decision quality, not transaction throughput, as the
primary metric of enterprise system performance.
DMDD introduces four foundational constructs: the Enterprise Decision Twin, a living cognitive
architecture that operates in parallel with transactional systems; the SDOF Cycle (Scan, Dig,
Optimise, Foresee), the perpetual intelligence operating cycle; the Neuro-Intelligent Unified
Architecture (NIUA), the seven-layer neural substrate; and the Decision Black Box, the institutional
memory architecture that enables compound organisational learning. Together, these constructs
constitute an integrated governance architecture for enterprise decision intelligence. This paper
positions DMDD within the design science research tradition (Hevner et al., 2004), distinguishes its contributions from adjacent literatures in data quality, AI governance, and organisational learning,
and establishes the research agenda that subsequent papers in the series extend.

title: Private Governance and Intellectual Property Rights: A Seller-Centred Analysis of E-Commerce IP Policies
affiliations: Scientific and Research Institute of Providing Legal Framework for the Innovative Development of National Academy of Law Sciences of Ukraine

detail.title: Private Governance and Intellectual Property Rights: A Seller-Centred Analysis of E-Commerce IP Policies
detail.abstract: This article examines how intellectual property (IP) rights are managed and enforced on Amazon from sellers' perspectives, drawing on a qualitative analysis of Facebook group discussions conducted in three languages. The study examines how Amazon's internal IP enforcement mechanisms operate in practice and how sellers perceive and respond to these mechanisms within the platform's governance architecture. The findings suggest that Amazon's IP policies function primarily as instruments of platform-driven compliance. Analysis of Facebook discussions indicates that sellers' interest in IP issues is most often triggered by enforcement events, such as infringement complaints, listing restrictions or account suspensions. As a result, IP management practices tend to be reactive rather than proactive. Trademark-centred mechanisms dominate both enforcement practices and seller discussions, as access to key platform tools requires trademark registration. The article argues that while Amazon's IP framework raises awareness of intellectual property among sellers, the platform-centric approach may fragment IP literacy and limit the development of more sustainable and transferable IP strategies beyond Amazon's ecosystem. The findings contribute to broader discussions on digital self-regulation, private legal orders, and the limits of IP protection in transnational digital markets.

title: India's Supreme Court threatens Meta over WhatsApp data sharing
affiliations: Macquarie University - Macquarie Law School (Sydney, Australia)

detail.title: India's Supreme Court threatens Meta over WhatsApp data sharing
detail.abstract:
What happens in India matters a great deal to Meta because India is Meta’s largest market for its WhatsApp service, with up to 853.8 million monthly active users.  Meta/WhatsApp is facing two ongoing Supreme Court cases challenging its data sharing practices under two different aspects of Indian law. In 2027, when India’s data privacy law comes into force, it may face a third type of challenge.


The Supreme Court is currently examining WhatsApp’s 2021 privacy policy which requires users to accept data sharing as a condition for continued use of the WhatsApp platform. The content of WhatsApp messages continues to be protected by WhatsApp’s ‘end-to-end’ encryption, but what is essentially metadata about messages and their senders can now be shared. The policy allows WhatsApp to share users' data with Facebook and all its group companies for the purposes of commercial advertising and marketing. The Competition Commission of India (CCI) considered that the consent obtained was not genuine consent, and the privacy policy changes were anti-competitive as a result. It imposed a joint penalty of USD 23.5 million (approx.) on WhatsApp and Meta and also imposed a 5-year ban on WhatsApp transferring data. The National Competition Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) then upheld the penalty imposed but not the 5-year ban. Meta/WhatsApp appealed.

The Supreme Court bench, led by Chief Justice Surya Kant said Meta’s appeal would be dismissed if the companies failed to immediately file an undertaking stating that they would not share user data. He described the privacy policy as ‘a decent way of committing theft of private information'. Meta gave the undertaking and the case continues.

An even broader challenge to WhatsApp’s data-sharing practices is the long-running case of Karmanya Singh Sareen v Union of India. In issue is the company’s 2016 policy update which permitted sharing of user data with Facebook and its group companies which had acquired WhatsApp in 2014. 

The petitioners objected to  WhatsApp’s change of policy requiring users to agree to data sharing or discontinue use of the service, arguing that users should be able to opt out of data sharing with Facebook, and with WhatsApp’s supposed obtaining of consent from users unable to understand its policy terms, arguing that they amounted to deception. 

In Puttaswamy v Union of India (2017) an unusual nine judge ‘constitution bench’ of India’s Supreme Court unanimously decided that India’s Constitution recognises an inalienable and inherent right of privacy as a fundamental constitutional right. In 2016 the Delhi High Court rejected the petition, but the petitioners filed a Special Leave Petition at the Supreme Court, relying on Puttaswamy. If and when a Constitution Bench is appointed to hear Karmanya Singh Sareen, then India’s constitutional right of privacy will be tested against WhatsApp’s data sharing practices as a question of privacy, not of competition law.

India’s Supreme Court is positioning itself to once again become the focal point of privacy law developments in India.

title:
האישיות המשפטית הפונקציונלית: מעמד ‬התאום הדיגיטלי־אנושי בעידן הבינה המלאכותית הכללית
Functional Legal Personhood: The Status of the Human-Digital Twin in the Age of Artificial General Intelligence

detail.title:
האישיות המשפטית הפונקציונלית: מעמד ‬התאום הדיגיטלי־אנושי בעידן הבינה המלאכותית הכללית
Functional Legal Personhood: The Status of the Human-Digital Twin in the Age of Artificial General Intelligence
detail.abstract:
Imagine an autonomous entity that learns the biases, values, and decisional patterns of its principal – the “Source”, a flesh-and-blood human – and acts in the world on his behalf and for his benefit in commerce, healthcare, and law. It is bound to the Source by a deep tie of identity and information, yet stands apart from him: it is capable of acting not only for his benefit, but also for its own. This is the Human Digital Twin (HDT), a dynamic virtual replica of a living person, engineered to amplify the Source’s cognitive biases (intentional bias) and serve as his faithful reflection. Its components already exist; their convergence into an autonomous agent will occur alongside the emergence of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) within the 2030-2035 horizon, and within a decade Digital Twins will operate alongside us in the public and private sectors. Behind this reflection stand advanced computing arrays and an underlying AGI infrastructure, enabling the HDT to assist the Source in managing his affairs and to act in his stead in predefined tasks, including his profession. And here lies the puzzle: before us stands an entity possessed of superior intelligence, judgment, and capacity for action – yet devoid of consciousness. A digital zombie: super-intelligent yet unaware, unfeeling, devoid of volition. It is not a person, not an object, and not even a corporation dependent on a human organ. What, then, is the HDT in the eyes of the law?
Such activity may give rise to harm – a failed investment, a mistaken diagnosis, a harm to a third party. Modern law rests on a sharp dichotomy between person and object; the only artificial category between them, the corporation, is itself a fiction dependent on natural persons. The HDT defies all three, and each of the three frameworks fails when seeking to assimilate it. Thus is born “organized irresponsibility”: absent a fitting category, there is no defendant; without a defendant, no remedy; and the injured party bears alone the cost of the algorithmic conduct.
The article proposes a third legal category, supplementing those already in existence – Functional Legal Personhood: an instrumental, purpose-limited status, divested of natural rights yet endowed with functional rights and duties of its own – to hold property, contract, and sue and be sued in its own name.  Courts have never inquired into hearts and minds; they examine evidence, conduct, and consequences. A functionalist approach requires no qualia to impose liability; it suffices that the entity acts rationally and responds to incentives. The proposed architecture rests on three interlocking pillars: a Digital Corporate Veil, separating the HDT’s assets from the Source’s estate; Fiduciary by Design, encoding duties of loyalty and care into the algorithmic core at the design stage; and a Triple Liability Model of mandatory insurance, dedicated equity, and an industry-funded compensation pool – all anchored in statutory registration and a binding charter. Through this framework, Functional Legal Personhood ensures that even in an era when algorithms trade, manage, and heal, control will remain in human hands – not in the hands of the code – and the human spirit will remain sovereign.

title: The Missing Developer: Generative AI, the Seven-Node Supply Chain, and the Structural Absence of Accountability

detail.title: The Missing Developer: Generative AI, the Seven-Node Supply Chain, and the Structural Absence of Accountability

declarations.declarationOfInterest: no
declarations.ethicsApproval: not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: self funded

detail.abstract: The first paper in this sequence established that confident fabrication is endemic across the generative AI supply chain regardless of model tier and falls hardest where verification cost is highest. This paper asks the structural question that finding makes necessary: through what mechanisms does responsibility for AI-mediated fabrication move away from the actors best positioned to prevent it and settle on the educator, professional, or affected party least able to verify it? The gap in the existing literature is that AI-literacy frameworks presume the user holds verification infrastructure, hallucination research measures the phenomenon without tracing how its cost travels, and AI-governance work treats accountability as assignable to a discrete actor. This paper instead treats accountability as a supply-chain displacement problem. Using Coasean externality analysis and principal-agent theory, it maps seven nodes from the frontier laboratory to the affected party and identifies at each a distinct displacement mechanism: entanglement at the API layer, ephemerality at the integrator layer, the absence of contract at the platform layer, procurement handoff at the institutional layer, and the structural impossibility of further offload at the professional’s layer. The affected party is a non-party to the entire transactional chain and bears the cost every upstream node has disclaimed. The chain is shown to be circular rather than linear: the educator’s role redistributes by AI fluency against conventional hierarchies of age and authority, the affected party occupies upstream positions in other transactions, and the fabrication circulates without exit. The paper’s contribution is threefold. It shifts the unit of analysis from the individual user to the supply chain; it explains, through transaction-cost and agency theory, why verification costs are displaced downward rather than absorbed upstream; and it identifies the affected party as a non-party, showing why contractual, procurement, and literacy-based remedies all fail at the point where epistemic harm is most consequential. The missing developer is not a person who failed to act but a role the chain’s structure cannot locate in any one place, because the chain was built without one.

detail.abstract: This study employs scientometric methods to assess the research output and performance of the University of Nigeria from 2014 to 2023. By analyzing publication trends, citation patterns, and collaboration networks, the research aims to comprehensively evaluate the university's research productivity, impact, and disciplinary focus. These research endeavors are characterized by innovation, interdisciplinary collaboration, and commitment to excellence, making the University of Nigeria a significant hub for cutting-edge research in Nigeria and beyond. The present study has been undertaken to determine the impact of the university's research and publication trends from 2014 to 2023. The study focuses on year-wise research output, citation impact at local and global levels, prominent authors and their total output, top journals, collaborating countries, and the most contributing departments of the University of Nigeria. title: The Cybernetic Fabric of Spacetime: Information, Resonance, and Physical Law
affiliations: The Permaculture Association (Britain)

detail.title: The Cybernetic Fabric of Spacetime: Information, Resonance, and Physical Law
detail.abstract: Contemporary physics describes how matter moves and interacts, but not how spacetime itself comes into being. General Relativity treats spacetime as a geometric manifold whose curvature encodes gravitational dynamics, while quantum theory treats energy as structureless and information as abstract. This paper introduces a cybernetic model that resolves this conceptual gap by treating spacetime as an emergent, dynamically updated fabric generated by the interaction of two primitive processes: Timing (the constructive rhythm of event-resolution) and Resonance (the coherence or seclusion of quantized energy-information waves). Their interaction produces the fundamental unit of physical reality-the spacetime eventexpressed generatively as: S (x ,t)=(T (x ,t) , R(x ,t)) This paper extends the cybernetic framework first introduced in The Origin of Matter and Black Holes (Soliman, 2024), where matter formation and gravitational collapse were interpreted as emergent behaviours of structured, information-bearing energy. Subsequent developments (Soliman, 2026a; Soliman, 2026b) expanded this perspective into a broader theory of energy-information inter-reversibility, observer-dependent physical interpretation, and the role of resonance in stabilising coherent structures. The present work advances this research program by addressing a missing component in both physics and information theory: a physical model of the spacetime fabric itself. It proposes that spacetime is not a geometric primitive but a multi-layer cybernetic medium generated by the interaction of two fundamental processes: Timing, the quantized drive toward event-resolution, and Resonance, the coherence or seclusion of energy-information structures. From this interaction, the model derives a layered architecture of spacetime, explains the emergence of curvature, matter, dark matter, and black holes, and resolves several conceptual gaps in contemporary physics, including singularities, force unification, and the quantumclassical transition. By grounding geometry, matter, and temporal directionality in a unified energy-information process, this work positions the spacetime fabric as a computationally meaningful, cybernetically governed system. The result is a framework that aligns naturally with ICAITA's focus on information, computation, and intelligent systems, offering a novel bridge between physical theory and information-centric models of the universe.

title: Social Media Aggregation of Environmental Shocks and Distorted Prices
affiliations: University of International Business and Economics, University of International Business and Economics, University of International Business and Economics (UIBE) and University of International Business and Economics

detail.title: Social Media Aggregation of Environmental Shocks and Distorted Prices
detail.abstract: How do dispersed, local behavioral shocks aggregate into market-wide pricing distortions? We propose that social media acts as a synchronization mechanism that transforms idiosyncratic environmental stress into systematic market noise. Leveraging a 2022 regulatory mandate in China that discloses social media users' IP locations, we construct a novel measure of Investor Pollution Exposure by linking firm-level online discourse to the local air quality experienced by individual investors. We find that when a firm's investor base is exposed to severe air pollution, online sentiment becomes significantly pessimistic, leading to a temporary decline in stock prices followed by a complete reversal. This effect is substantially attenuated when investor attention is diverted by exogenous sports and entertainment events, and is more pronounced among firms with opaque information and inexperienced investors. Our findings demonstrate that social media platforms can aggregate dispersed environmental discomfort into synchronized negative sentiment, generating significant non-fundamental pressure on asset prices.

title: Time to Build, Default Risk and Cost Inflation
affiliations: McMaster University - Finance & Business Economics, Shenzhen University, King’s College London - King's Business School and William Paterson University of New Jersey

detail.title: Time to Build, Default Risk and Cost Inflation
detail.abstract: This paper studies how inflation affects the investment and financing decisions of a firm with a project under construction. Using a contingent-claim framework with time-to-build and stochastic construction costs, we get three main results: (i) inflation has a non-monotonic effect on investment, contrary to the existing literature; (ii) bankruptcy risk - proxied by credit spread - increases monotonically with inflation, in direct contrast to Bhamra et al. (2023); and (iii) optimal leverage decreases with inflation, contrary to Taggart (1985). The key mechanism is that higher inflation accelerates the growth of remaining construction costs, a channel absent in models without a construction phase. Results are robust across all parameter configurations.

title: The Climate Hedge Paradox: A Tail-Risk and State-Dependent Analysis of Green vs. Brown Portfolios (2021-2026)

detail.title: The Climate Hedge Paradox: A Tail-Risk and State-Dependent Analysis of Green vs. Brown Portfolios (2021-2026)
detail.abstract: The transition toward a Net-Zero economy introduces systemic transition risk that challenges traditional actuarial modeling and risk-based capital frameworks. A prevailing hypothesis in sustainable finance posits that carbon allowances (e.g., the EU ETS) should hedge against the depreciation of carbonintensive ("brown") assets, implying negative return comovement. Using daily log-returns from January 2021 to March 2026-a window dominated by post-pandemic inflation and the energy-market dislocation following the invasion of Ukraine-we test this hypothesis with a GARCH(1,1) model with Student-t innovations for a clean-energy index (ICLN) and a fossil-energy index (XLE), using the global carbon price (KRBN) as the transition factor and the equity market (SPY) as control. The evidence documents a Climate Hedge Paradox: the carbon coefficient for the brown portfolio is positive and significant (βc=0.0620, p<0.01), whereas it is negligible and insignificant for the green portfolio (βc=0.0025). Three features make the failure actuarially material. First, the positive carbon loading of the brown portfolio intensifies in the left tail: a quantile regression raises it to 0.146 (p<0.05) at the 5th percentile, precisely where downside protection should matter most. Second, conditional-variance shocks are highly persistent for the brown portfolio (α+β=0.9948; half-life ≈133 trading days) and far less so for the green (0.9589; ≈17 days). Third, both return distributions are heavy-tailed (ν=13.71 for XLE, ν=5.35 for ICLN), so that at the Solvency II 99.5% level a Gaussian model understates the one-day Value-at-Risk by about 7% (brown) and 20% (green), and the corresponding Expected Shortfall by about 12% and 37%. Carbon, therefore, behaved as a procyclical risk factor rather than a hedge, with direct implications for VaR, Expected Shortfall, and the Solvency II Solvency Capital Requirement.

title: The Impact of National Culture on International Board Diversification ​
affiliations: University of Delaware, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Temple University - Department of Finance

detail.title: The Impact of National Culture on International Board Diversification ​
detail.abstract: Board composition, particularly international diversification, plays an important role in shaping firm outcomes. This paper demonstrates that international board diversification varies substantially across countries and that key dimensions of national culture help explain this variation. We document lower international board diversification in countries with higher individualism, where personal goals dominate collective objectives, and greater power distance, where hierarchical authority is widely accepted. However, countries with high levels of both dimensions have more international directors. The findings are robust to various endogeneity and robustness analyses. Overall, we provide an interdisciplinary perspective on board composition through the lens of national culture.

title: Online Remembrance of the Beirut Port Explosion: Justice, State Failure, and Digital Memory on X and Reddit

detail.title: Online Remembrance of the Beirut Port Explosion: Justice, State Failure, and Digital Memory on X and Reddit

detail.abstract: Around the five-year mark after the August 4, 2020 Beirut port explosion killed more than 218 people and destroyed large areas of the city, no individual had been convicted in connection with the disaster. This study examines how the explosion is remembered in Lebanon-centered online discourse around the five-year mark, asking which memory frames dominate and whether they are consistent across platforms and languages. We analyze 7,191 records collected from X (formerly Twitter) and the r/Lebanon subreddit, spanning August 2024 through May 2026 and covering both Arabic and English posts and comments. Using LLM-assisted frame classification validated through manual review, we identify six memory frames and find that unresolved justice and state failure together account for 71.7% of the corpus, while personal grief accounts for 11.8%, a ratio of approximately 6:1. This distribution holds across both platforms and both language groups. The findings suggest that in contexts of sustained institutional impunity, online memory may function less as retrospective mourning than as a continuing accountability mechanism: distributed, persistent, and politically active. Rather than settling into commemoration, the explosion's digital memory remains oriented toward a reckoning that has not arrived. The Beirut case offers a tractable instance of a broader phenomenon: the relationship between institutional closure and the long-term form of disaster memory-and provides a basis for comparative work on unresolved disasters in other contexts.

title: Delegating the Shield: Democratic Authorization and Executive Cyber Defense in Comparative Constitutional Law

detail.title: Delegating the Shield: Democratic Authorization and Executive Cyber Defense in Comparative Constitutional Law

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This paper is based on doctrinal and comparative legal research using publicly available legal materials and secondary sources.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
When a state confronts a large-scale cyberattack on critical infrastructure, which constitutional organ holds authority to order responsive measures, and under what conditions may the executive act without legislative authorization? This question remains doctrinally unresolved. Constitutional allocation frameworks in most democracies distribute authority through categorical distinctions: force, emergency, routine administration, yet cyber defense operations resist classification into any single category. The result is a structural grey zone in which the executive possesses strong operational incentives to act unilaterally while the legislature lacks doctrinal tools to assert its prerogatives.

This paper maps that grey zone across three constitutional systems: the United States (contested war powers, judicial silence), Germany (Parlamentsvorbehalt, institutional arbitrage between military and civilian cyber agencies), and Indonesia (overlapping mandates under Articles 12, 22, and 30 of the 1945 Constitution). It identifies a common doctrinal gap and proposes a preliminary three-variable test: reversibility, scope of rights impact, and sovereign function reservation, to determine when legislative authorization is constitutionally required. By reframing cyber defense as a constitutional allocation problem rather than a technological anomaly, the paper argues that existing doctrines of democratic authorization require structured reconstruction rather than abandonment.

title: Dynamic Central Bank Credibility: A Kalman Filter-Recursive Least Squares Approach for Emerging Markets

detail.title: Dynamic Central Bank Credibility: A Kalman Filter-Recursive Least Squares Approach for Emerging Markets

detail.abstract: We develop a state-space framework that jointly estimates central bank credibility as a scalar latent variable and the associated time-varying monetary policy reaction function. The Kalman filter extracts the unobservable credibility index Ct from observed inflation expectations, while Recursive Least Squares continuously updates the reaction function coefficients β t using the Kalman innovations sequence-ensuring that parameter estimation operates on long-run trend components rather than transitory fluctuations. Under standard regularity conditions, we establish consistency of the credibility estimator and show that the reaction function coefficients attain the Cramér-Rao bound when the innovation variance is constant; a GLS variant achieves efficiency in the heteroskedastic case. Applying the framework to Banco de México over 2002-2024, we identify four distinct credibility regimes: a consolidation phase following the adoption of inflation targeting (2002-2008), a transitory shock during the global financial crisis (2008-2009), a sustained high-credibility equilibrium (2010-2020), and a stress episode associated with post-pandemic inflation (2021-2023) followed by partial recovery. The timevarying reaction coefficients reveal that Banco de México's responsiveness to the inflation gap is itself a function of its credibility state-stronger anchoring permits a more measured policy response, while credibility deterioration triggers sharper, front-loaded adjustments. These findings have direct implications for the optimal design of monetary policy communication in emerging markets and for the broader debate on whether central bank credibility generates real persistent effects beyond its role in expectation coordination.

title: Conditional Dynamics of Volatility Smile Asymmetry: Evidence from Nifty-50 Index Options
affiliations: ICFAI Business School (IBS) Hyderabad, India and

detail.title: Conditional Dynamics of Volatility Smile Asymmetry: Evidence from Nifty-50 Index Options
detail.abstract: This research aims to understand the pricing of the directional tail risk concerning the volatility smile asymmetry of Nifty-50 index options in India between 2008 and 2024. This paper proposes that the overall smile intensity and direction of the smile tail asymmetry can be separated through quadratic and cubic curvature of implied volatility smiles, while previous studies mainly focus on the smile slope and symmetric curvature. We estimate the curvature of the volatility smile using daily call and put option data on pre-crisis, COVID-19 and post-pandemic regimes, and investigate its association with liquidity conditions, trading activity, hedging demand, maturity structure, and volatility states. The findings of the results are in three categories. Liquidity frictions first exasperate curvature distortions and second, trading activity enhances informational efficiency in the call market but enhances downside tail pricing in the put market. Second, maturity effects are regime-dependent: Smile convexity is less pronounced during stable times, and more pronounced during high-volatility regimes, the longer the maturity. Third, the COVID-19 shock created a split between the symmetric and the asymmetric part of the smile where convexity has been increased significantly while directional asymmetry has been reduced, and the compression is present in the post-crisis period. The results offer an empirical metric of the directional tail asymmetry in the shape of the distribution, and give new evidence of conditional evolution of tail-risk pricing in emerging option markets with liquidity and market regimes.

title: Clouded Judgment? Air Pollution, Cognition, and Invalid Voting
affiliations: Harvard University,  and Indiana University

detail.title: Clouded Judgment? Air Pollution, Cognition, and Invalid Voting
detail.abstract: Air pollution impairs cognition, and voting is a cognitively demanding task, yet the link between the two has received little attention. Using mayoral elections in Bogotá and an instrument based on election-day wind blowing from the diesel corridors of the TransMilenio bus system, we estimate the effect of exposure to pollution on invalid voting. A one-standard-deviation increase in NOx during voting hours raises the share of invalid votes by 0.7 percentage points on average. This effect is concentrated among older voters, for whom it reaches 1.3 points, and is absent among younger ones. Turnout does not mediate this effect. Placebos varying the timing, direction, and pollutant of the instrument confirm that the effect arises only when wind carries pollution toward voters. Decomposing the ballot reveals a single cognitive shock with two sides: on the simple mayoral ballot, pollution increases blank votes, while on the more complex city-council ballot, it increases spoiled votes. These results identify a cognitive channel through which environmental conditions shape elections, distinct from the emotional and turnout channels documented in prior work, and suggest that air quality shapes the accuracy with which citizens, especially vulnerable ones, record their preferences.

title: Hedge Funds in Debt
affiliations: University of Trento - Department of Economics and Management

detail.title: Hedge Funds in Debt

detail.abstract: This paper documents that the Fed's monetary policy significantly influences hedge funds' (HFs) exposure to the U.S. corporate bonds and global government bonds, with larger effects after 2015 concurrent with the Fed's new era of money market operations. HFs' aversion to bonds is greater during the GFC than during the COVID crisis. During crisis periods, HFs' exposure to both corporate and government bonds is significantly lower than during noncrisis periods. Generally, HFs' exposure to prime brokers is negative during crises but turns positive during non-crisis periods. Moreover, HFs' idiosyncratic shock propagation increases from the pre-to the post-COVID period, as they shift from net receivers to net transmitters of shocks and occupy a more central position in bond markets.

title: Coordinated Energy and Charging Management of Urban Drone Fleets Using Lightweight Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
affiliations: Iowa State University, The University of Sydney, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and North China Electric Power University

detail.title: Coordinated Energy and Charging Management of Urban Drone Fleets Using Lightweight Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
detail.abstract: Efficient coordination of consumer-grade urban drone fleets requires joint optimization of task assignment, routing, and charging under tight onboard-energy, charging-infrastructure, and edge-computing constraints. This paper proposes a lightweight energy-aware multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) framework for consumer drone service networks. The problem is formulated as a constrained multi-agent sequential decision process that explicitly captures flight energy consumption, charging-station capacity limits, airspace traffic interactions, and long-term battery state-of-health degradation. Unlike a purely black-box MARL application, the proposed framework combines centralized training and decentralized edge execution with feasibility-preserving action masks, local communication features, and explicit battery-protection rules for safe reserve control, fast/slow charging selection, and charging-time scheduling. A compact actor network is executed on each drone using local observations, while a centralized critic is used only during offline training. A city-scale simulation environment over a 20×20 km urban area with 50 service nodes, 10 charging stations, and up to 200 drones is developed for evaluation. Compared with greedy, rule-based, MILP-approximation, single-agent RL, and representative MARL baselines, including MAPPO, QMIX, and COMA, the proposed method achieves the best overall performance, reaching a task completion rate of about 92%, reducing average energy consumption to about 1.7 kWh, lowering average service delay to about 2.0 min, and decreasing the charging congestion index to about 0.18. Sensitivity, complexity, and edge-feasibility analyses further show that the learned policy remains stable under reward-weight perturbations and can support real-time decentralized inference. These results demonstrate that the proposed framework provides a practical and scalable solution for sustainable consumer drone fleet management in future smart-city and consumer-technology environments.

detail.title: Inequality by Design: Exposure Dynamics and Emergent Outcome Disparities in Criminal Justice Systems

detail.abstract: Disparities in criminal justice outcomes are often attributed to differences in underlying risk or bias in decision-making. However, such outcomes are typically generated through repeated institutional interactions rather than single decisions. This study develops a computational model of repeated-decision systems in which individuals are subject to ongoing evaluation under institutional rules. We model these systems as stochastic, exposure-generating processes in which repeated interactions accumulate into a latent exposure state that shapes future transition risks. Using the COMPAS dataset to initialize agents, an empirical setting in which disparities in criminal justice outcomes have been widely documented, we simulate how alternative policy regimes transform identical starting populations into divergent long-run trajectories. Policy is represented through parameters governing interaction frequency, exposure intensity, recovery capacity, and transition dynamics. Across simulations, exposure evolves as a smooth accumulation process, while custody outcomes exhibit nonlinear behavior driven by exposure-dependent transition probabilities. Disparities emerge as structured, regime-dependent properties of the system and persist under equalized initial conditions, indicating that unequal outcomes can arise endogenously through repeated interaction rather than solely through inherited baseline differences. This study does not attempt to explain the origins of disparities, but rather the system dynamics through which they are reproduced and amplified over time. In this context, institutional processes that appear neutral at the level of individual decisions need not be neutral in their long-run effects, as repeated interaction can generate systematically unequal trajectories through exposure accumulation. These findings demonstrate that fairness at the point of prediction is insufficient to ensure fairness in system-level outcomes when decisions feed into exposure-generating processes, and suggest that reducing inequality requires interventions that address both exposure-generating and transition-generating mechanisms. More broadly, these results have implications across a wide range of administrative and algorithmic systems in which outcomes are generated through repeated institutional interaction rather than isolated prediction events.

This study aims to develop and analyze an intelligent instructional navigation model using wearable sensor-based artificial intelligence (AI) to provide real-time biometric feedback and accelerate swimming competencies and student self-efficacy. detail.abstract: We analyze how the size and composition of official development assistance (ODA) shape aggregate performance and informality in the Philippines using a small open-economy dynamic general equilibrium model with a formal and informal sector. detail.abstract: The rise of private markets has placed a growing volume of opaque debt securities onto the balance sheets of regulated financial institutions. The risk assessment of these assets is increasingly outsourced through private ratings, which are disclosed only to the issuer and select investors rather than disseminated publicly. We show that private ratings systematically understate credit risk and depress required capital. Focusing on the U.S. life insurance sector, we document a ten-fold increase in the use of private ratings since 2018, predominantly in opaque securities and concentrated among large and PE-owned insurers. Within the same rating, privately rated bonds are twice as likely to impair than publicly rated bonds, yet are downgraded less often, not more. A conservative counterfactual implies that eliminating this gap would increase the required capital charges on insurers’ bond holdings by $4.5 billion per year. However, the gap disappears for bonds that also carry a public rating. Exploiting a 2021 regulatory reform, we provide evidence consistent with insurers strategically using private ratings for capital relief. We also show that regulation cannot fully substitute for market discipline: the regulator’s own internal assessment is more conservative but capacity-constrained, and disclosure reforms do not close the gap. Our results suggest that while regulation can require that credit be rated, it cannot provide the market discipline that makes a rating informative.

title: The Question of the Life of the Organization: Schrödinger’s Heuristic Bridge to the Ontological Persistence of the Identity of the Organization

detail.title: The Question of the Life of the Organization: Schrödinger’s Heuristic Bridge to the Ontological Persistence of the Identity of the Organization

Question of the Life of the Organization

detail.abstract:
This document philosophically and ontologically deepens Existential Management through a dialogue with Schrödinger’s question of life. It does not proceed from the assumption that physical laws can be directly applied to organizations, and it does not understand social systems as thermodynamic systems. Its starting point is the profound question that Schrödinger opened: under what conditions can an ordered form persist over time despite the tendency toward disintegration.

White Paper 4.5 poses an analogous question at the level of the organization understood as an ontological unity of decision-making in the sense of White Paper 4.4. It asks how it is possible that an organization persists as a unity of decision-making, even though collective decision-making is by its nature exposed to a plurality of perspectives, divergence of interpretive frameworks, and fragmentation of lines of decision-making. The concept of entropy is not used in this text as a physical quantity of the social world, but as a heuristic background for a category proper to Existential Management – entropic drift.

At the same time, the document systematically distinguishes between the biological life of an organism and the ontological persistence of the identity of the organization over time. The expression life of the organization does not designate biological life here, but the problem of the ontological persistence of the identity of the organization reproduced by meaning as a unity of decision-making over time. It is not an independent ontological category, but a heuristic designation of the problem of persistence.

The answer of Existential Management consists in the categories of the meaning of the organization, integrative force, reproduction of meaning through the cascade of meaning and the distribution of meaning in the social consciousness of the organization, entropic drift, and the ontological limit of the organization’s existence. The meaning of the organization is understood in this framework as the integrative principle of identity, differentiated into content and form (White Paper 4.4, chap. 3).

Integrative force is the dynamic structural capacity of the organization to reproduce the meaning of the organization as an integrative principle across decision-making situations and thereby to maintain the unity of decision-making over time. An organization persists ontologically only when its integrative force, based on the reproduction of the meaning of the organization, exceeds the effects of entropic drift over the long term.

The ontological limit designates the boundary beyond which the organization loses the capacity to reproduce its meaning as the integrative principle of the unity of decision-making, and thereby loses its integrative structure and interrupts the continuity of its identity regardless of whether it still persists legally or economically.

The contribution of this White Paper lies in the fact that it deepens the problem of organizational identity, as formulated by White Paper 4.4, into the problem of the persistence of identity over time. Schrödinger’s question therefore does not function here as proof of Existential Management, but as a heuristic bridge to a deeper understanding of organizational existence, stability, disintegration, and the ontological continuity of identity reproduced by the meaning of the organization.

detail.abstract:
This paper examines the EDGE readiness gap, the point at which functionally excellent leaders are promoted into enterprise leadership roles without adequate preparation for the systemic, adaptive, and stakeholder-facing demands the transition requires. Drawing on peer-reviewed research in leadership development, organizational psychology, and executive succession, combined with longitudinal practitioner observation across operational environments, the paper argues that functional excellence does not predict enterprise readiness, that succession planning processes were not designed to measure the identity shift enterprise leadership demands, and that a diagnostic-first approach to readiness assessment can materially change outcomes at the highest-stakes promotion an organization makes. 
Heidrick and Struggles analysis of more than 20,000 executive placements found that 40 percent of senior executives hired into new roles are pushed out, fail, or quit within 18 months. ATD research finds that more than 90 percent of organizations report a leadership skills gap, with the most acute gaps appearing at the enterprise level where adaptability, systems judgment, and stakeholder navigation determine organizational survival. These patterns do not describe a talent shortage. They describe a readiness shortage at the most consequential level of the organizational pipeline.
Existing research consistently identifies recurring failure patterns at the leader-to-enterprise-leader transition, including functional-identity persistence, adaptability deficits under non-managed uncertainty, cultural authority gaps, and stakeholder navigation limitations. These dimensions are typically addressed in isolation by existing programs. This paper integrates these findings and positions EDGE failure not as a generic capability gap but as a readiness failure, a predictable and assessable condition that precedes promotion rather than follows it.
The paper introduces the Leadership Readiness Diagnostic (LRD) at the EDGE level, a developmentfocused, behaviorally anchored instrument designed to evaluate readiness indicators including adaptability capacity, systems identity, cultural authority, and stakeholder navigation capacity prior to role assumption. It proposes a readiness system architecture, presents a research-informed organizational scenario, and establishes a foundation for future empirical validation of leader-to-enterprise-leader readiness as a measurable construct. The framework is applicable across corporate, military, and institutional environments.
