detail.abstract: Primary healthcare systems in many developed countries are under strain, partly due to unrestricted patient demand. In response, policymakers have introduced measures to curb unnecessary GP visits, including (i) instituting a small upfront fee for GP visits, (ii) implementing a self-report based triage system, and (iii) providing more information to patients about their condition before they make an appointment with their GP. We evaluate the effectiveness of these approaches using two online experiments with a representative sample of UK adults. The first experiment involves induced monetary incentives in a laboratory-style study while the second is a health-framed vignette study. We find that while all three interventions are effective in the laboratory study, only the intervention that provides patients with more information about their condition reduces low-priority demand in the vignette study. We discuss implications for policy and for the study of health-related decision-making.

detail.abstract:
Paper 1 demonstrated that Collective Brain models fail to explain the origin of paradigm-shifting novelty from 500 BCE to 2026 CE.

This paper surveys the entire landscape those models cannot map, and proposes Heustoc Theory as the unifying successor framework. Heustoc combines two mechanisms:

(a) Heuristic Generation, the directional production of novelty through practical insight, rule-of-thumb reasoning, or guided search; and…

(b) Stochastic selection/Filtering, the survival or rejection of those novelties through contingency, repetition, institutional pressure, power, adoption, and historical timing.

We pre-empt the objection that unified theories overreach by deriving boundary conditions from real-time diffusion data. Real-time saturation dynamics from Paper 1 (n=475, D/V=89.9%, d²D/dt²<0 as of 22-May-26 23:20 IST) validate the model before peer review.

Using comparative historical analysis across scientific discovery, invention, language, ritual, faith, conquest, peer-review failure, flat-Earth persistence, and AI generation, we show that collective systems amplify, stabilize, or suppress novelty, but do not explain how it first appears or why it survives.

Heustoc is proposed as a compact and general explanatory framework for the emergence and retention of new forms across history and technology.

detail.abstract:
This Article introduces the theory of post-supremacy federalism to describe a structural condition in which federal law remains formally binding, but enforcement has durably receded or collapsed. Unlike frameworks grounded in intergovernmental friction or negotiated cooperation, this account begins from federal retreat—the cumulative erosion of enforcement capacity across judicial, administrative, legislative, and executive institutions. Post-supremacy federalism arises when three conditions are met: (1) federal law remains intact; (2) enforcement retreats; and (3) no formal devolution occurs. In this vacuum, states are not merely filling gaps. They are governing by default—under laws that still bind but no longer structure governance in a coherent or consistent way.

This Article maps the institutional dynamics behind this transformation, including judicial realignment, administrative collapse, legislative paralysis, and the rise of executive unilateralism. It then traces how this retreat manifests in four domains: drug policy, public education, environmental protection, and reproductive healthcare. In each, federal authority persists in theory, but meaningful enforcement has eroded—leaving states to construct and implement their own legal regimes without delegation, partnership, or protection. These domains are not newly decentralized. They are abandoned. Statutes like the Controlled Substances Act, Title IX, the Clean Air Act, and EMTALA remain binding, yet no longer coordinate or constrain state action. In their place, states exercise contingent authority—governing under conditions of legal precarity and enforcement asymmetry, exposed to federal snapback and forced to navigate an unstable landscape.

This Article does not propose reform. It offers a diagnosis. Post-supremacy federalism names the legal condition that emerges when federal authority recedes but does not relinquish control. Naming that condition is the first step toward understanding how governance now unfolds—and what may come next.

detail.abstract:
Background: Lebanon has endured a severe financial crisis since 2019, compounded by the COVID-19 pandemic and the August 2020 Beirut port explosion. These overlapping crises disrupted medication supply chains and care continuity for patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD). Secondary and tertiary hyperparathyroidism—key complications of CKD mineral and bone disorder (CKD-MBD)—require consistent medical management to prevent progression to parathyroidectomy. We examined whether the Lebanese financial crisis was associated with changes in parathyroidectomy incidence and cost among hemodialysis patients.

Methods: This single-centre retrospective cohort study included 52 adult hemodialysis patients at the LAUMC-RH unit in Beirut (2016–2023). Parathyroidectomy rates per 100 person-years were compared across pre-crisis (2016–2019) and post-crisis (2019–2023) periods using Poisson rate comparison. Multivariable Poisson regression identified independent predictors of parathyroidectomy. Surgical costs were compared using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test with 1,000-iteration bootstrap resampling.

Findings: Eleven parathyroidectomies were performed (4 pre-crisis, 7 post-crisis). Rates did not differ significantly between periods (4·5 vs 4·1 per 100 person-years; rate ratio 1·10, 95% CI 0·24–4·32; p=1·00). On multivariable analysis, older age was the only significant predictor of lower parathyroidectomy likelihood (RR 0·94, 95% CI 0·895–0·992; p=0·019). Medication access was largely preserved; 90% of patients continued CKD-MBD therapy throughout the crisis period. Median surgical costs escalated nearly 50-fold, from 4·3 million Lebanese pounds (LBP) pre-crisis to 210 million LBP post-crisis (p=0·017; bootstrap 95% CI 51·6 to 357·75 million LBP).

Interpretation: Despite Lebanon’s financial collapse, parathyroidectomy rates among hemodialysis patients remained stable, likely reflecting preserved medication access through adaptive patient- and centre-level strategies alongside structural constraints on surgical capacity. In contrast, the financial burden of parathyroidectomy escalated catastrophically, transforming a previously accessible intervention into an unaffordable one for most patients. These findings underscore the urgent need for innovative healthcare financing models, external donor support, and cross-national collaborations to safeguard access to essential surgical interventions for dialysis patients in fragile health systems.

title: Bank Run Contagion Through Social Network

detail.title: Bank Run Contagion Through Social Network
detail.abstract: This paper examines how social networks transmit bank runs, exploiting the 2023 U.S. banking crisis as a natural experiment. Leveraging Facebook's Social Connectedness Index and a difference-indifferences design, we find that banks in socially connected counties experience significantly lower deposit growth post-crisis, while geographic proximity shows no effect. Social contagion amplifies fundamental vulnerabilities, particularly for banks with high uninsured deposits and large held-to-maturity securities. However, exploiting within-bank variation reveals that fundamentals alone cannot explain the patterns: deposit outflows vary based on local social exposure even after controlling for all bank characteristics. Together, these results indicate that social contagion operates through both rational fundamental screening and panic-driven runs. We document a flight-to-safety: uninsured deposits flee while insured deposits flow in. Finally, socially-transmitted deposit shocks lead to significant credit supply contractions in both small business and mortgage lending, demonstrating substantial real economic consequences.

detail.abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive empirical and theoretical analysis of the transformative impact of Artificial Intelligence (AI) on global economic structures over the decade spanning 2025 to 2035, with a particular focus on the critical juncture of 2030-which marks the 25th-year quarter within the modern centennial economic cycle (1930-2030). Drawing upon longitudinal macroeconomic data, computational modeling, and cross-sectional analysis of 47 economies across six continents, this study examines AI's multidimensional role in reshaping GDP trajectories, labor markets, financial systems, industrial productivity, and inter-nation economic competitiveness. Our findings indicate that economies with robust AI infrastructure investment will experience cumulative GDP gains of 14-23% above baseline projections by 2030, while nations lagging in AI adoption face compounding structural deficits. The study introduces the Economic Intelligence Transformation Index (EITI) as a novel composite metric for measuring AI-driven economic readiness. Furthermore, we analyze the historical 100-year economic quarter-a supercycle lens spanning four generational economic paradigm shifts-and situate AI as the dominant disruptive force of the fourth industrial revolution, analogous to electrification in the 1920s. Policy implications, distributional consequences, and governance frameworks are discussed with actionable recommendations for governments, central banks, and multilateral institutions.

Background: Existing ALS prognostic models rely on biomarkers with marked ethnic variability and provide risk categories rather than individualised probabilities, limiting their generalisability across populations and full ALS phenotype spectrum.

Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of 833 patients enrolled at First Affiliated Hospital of Xi'an Jiaotong University. The training cohort included 532 patients (2010–2020), and the temporal external validation cohort included 301 patients (2021–2024). Prognostic factors were identified by Parametric Survival Model. A nomogram was constructed and validated through internal bootstrapping and external validation. Model performance was assessed by area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), calibration, and decision curve analysis (DCA).

Findings: Seven independent prognostic factors were identified: age of onset, sex, diagnostic delay time, ALSFRS-R, interval time onset-second involvement region, region of onset, and Awaji-Shima Criteria. The nomogram showed excellent discrimination (internal validation AUC: 0.871 for 3-year and 0.833 for 5-year; external validation AUC: 0.848 for 3-year), strong calibration, and net clinical benefit on DCA. 

Interpretation: This nomogram, covering all ALS phenotypes in a Chinese cohort, demonstrated discrimination nominally higher than the landmark van den Berg model (3-year AUC 0.848 vs 0.78) using seven routine variables without genetic or biomarker data. Individualised risk estimates may enable patient stratification in clinical trials, where phenotypic heterogeneity contributes to failures beyond ALSFRS-R slope. detail.abstract:
Background Low appendicular skeletal muscle (ASM) predicts adverse health outcomes in European, North American and East Asian populations. Few studies have examined ASM amongst South Asians, a major global population group recognized to have high rates of abdominal obesity and increased cardiometabolic risk.

Methods We investigated 197,066 participants of South Asia Biobank (SAB), a population-based study of men and women aged 18-80 years, living in Bangladesh, India, Pakistan, and Sri Lanka. ASM was measured by bio-impedance. Normative ranges for height-adjusted (ASM/Ht2) and BMI-adjusted (ASM/BMI) muscle mass were developed amongst 129,801 initially healthy participants. Associations between ASM indices and all-cause mortality were assessed in a longitudinal sub-cohort of 24,874 participants followed longitudinally (median 4·5 years).  

Findings Our derived thresholds for low ASM were similar to published criteria in men, but substantially lower than those reported in women. Among participants aged 41 to 80 years, low ASM was present in 9·3% of men and 2·5% of women based on ASM/Ht2, and 7·1% and 2·3% in men and women respectively based on ASM/BMI. Older age and male sex were associated with increased risk of low ASM. The associations of low ASM with overweight and obesity were directionally opposite for ASM/BMI compared to ASM/Ht2, indicating these measures capture divergent muscle mass phenotypes. There were 1,447 deaths among the 24,874 participants followed longitudinally. Low ASM was a risk factor for all-cause mortality based on our ASM/Ht2 threshold (1·37 [1·15-1·64], P<0·001) but not based on published criteria.

Interpretation We provide a robust framework for assessment of skeletal muscle mass in South Asians, and the basis for future studies investigating the etiology and clinical significance of low muscle mass in South Asia.

detail.title: Extreme Events in Corporate Bond Spreads
detail.abstract: The market value of corporate bonds was equivalent to around a third of global GDP as of 2024. It represents a key asset class for professional and private investors. However, it is subject to high volatility and is very sensitive to rare but extreme events, such as the financial and Covid-19 crises. We study the extremal behaviour of corporate bond spreads in the United States and in the Euro Area across different rating segments and sectors. We base our study on three decades of daily data. We control for financial and macroeconomic variables that are likely to affect spreads. Our approach uses three different methods from Extreme Value Theory (EVT). It focuses first on the marginal distributions of corporate bond spreads, then models the bivariate tail dependence structure of cross-regional and cross-market corporate bond spreads and finally on the distribution of corporate bond spreads over time, capturing their volatility dynamics as well as their heavy tails. During crisis periods, the degree of dependence is surprisingly high, suggesting a contagion effect. Our fitted models show that more standard approaches would massively underestimate the probabilities of rare events and that the combination of dynamic volatility modelling with EVT is robust and well suited for extrapolating risk measures beyond the maximum level of corporate bond spreads observed in the historical data.

Background: Nearly half of all global stillbirths occur in sub-Saharan Africa, underscoring the need to identify pregnant women at higher risk of stillbirth in these settings. However, despite the increasing number of studies developing stillbirth prediction models in the region, external validation and model updating remain limited.

Methods:  In this prognostic modelling study, we externally validated and updated an existing stillbirth prediction model originally developed in Uganda. The existing model included five obstetric history predictors. We used the ALERT project e-registry dataset, collected from 16 hospitals across Benin, Malawi, Tanzania, and Uganda. After external validation, and recalibration of the existing model, we employed mixed effects logistic regression to re-estimate the existing model’s coefficients and extended the model by incorporating five additional predictors available at admission. Model performance was assessed through discrimination, calibration, classification measures and decision curve analyses. Internal-external cross-validation was applied to the extended model and the performance measures were summarised using random-effects meta-analysis.

Findings:  The validation dataset included 134,368 pregnant women. The rate of stillbirth was 3·8%. External validation of the existing prediction model demonstrated poor discrimination with an AUROC of 0·53 (95% CI: 0·52 - 0·54). Recalibration of the model did not improve the AUROC. The apparent performance after model re-estimation demonstrated an AUROC of 0·71 (95% CI: 0·70- 0·72). The extended model sustained good discrimination after the internal-external cross-validation with a pooled AUROC of 0·73 (95% CI: 0·69 - 0·76) (Tau2 = 0·00). The pooled calibration-in-the-large was 0·00 (95% CI: -0·24 - 0·25), however, the large between-hospital variance (Tau2= 0·25) suggests pronounced differences in baseline risk.

Interpretation: The external validation demonstrated limited generalisability of the existing Ugandan model. Re-estimation and extension of the model showed improved discrimination and calibration. However, additional external validation and local recalibration are required before the extended model can be implemented clinically.

detail.title: Investment composition and growth: the role of intangible and tangible ICT capital in the EU and other economies
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether differences in the composition of investment help explain economic growth disparities in the EU and other advanced economies from 1996 to 2021. While overall investment levels in the EU and the US are broadly similar, the EU invests less in intangible and tangible ICT capital. This difference in composition is associated with part of the EU’s productivity gap with the US. Employing panel fixed effects and local projection methods, we find that intangible and tangible ICT investments -particularly in communications equipment, R&D, and other intellectual property products- are associated with higher GDP per capita growth than other forms of investment. To quantify these differences, we construct a novel investment efficiency ratio that relates the estimated economic growth contribution of each asset to its share in total investment. The results are robust across empirical methods, country samples, and time periods, and reveal substantial heterogeneity: the growth association of ICT-related investment is stronger in countries with higher income levels and greater human capital. Overall, the findings suggest that improving the allocation and efficiency of investment, rather than simply increasing its volume, is key to enhancing long-term growth.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a formally specified, scale-invariant framework for the analysis, diagnosis, and design of innovation ecosystems, grounded in a causal model of how cultural authorization conditions and stakeholder configurations produce Capability-Knowledge Coherence across nested ecosystem levels. The framework introduces the Innovation Ecosystem Matrix (IEM) — a three-dimensional instrument that maps innovation activity through two orthogonal axes (WHY: Vision-Driven vs. Need-Driven; HOW: Focused vs. Progressive) producing four universal quadrants (Basic Research, Technology Development, Value Venture, Organizational Scaling), and a formally specified third dimension, the Ecosystem Context Model (ECM). The ECM operates through two causal layers — Cultural Envelope and Stakeholder Depth — producing Capability-Knowledge Coherence as a derived output across three scale levels (Macro, Meso, Micro) and nine named cells. A twelve-dimension scoring instrument operationalizes the ECM through a four-step non-compensatory aggregation methodology grounded in Leontief's (1941) input-output theory, with corroborating precedents in behavioral decision science (Simon, 1955; Tversky, 1972; Kahneman & Tversky, 1979), institutional diagnostics (PEFA, 2016), and innovation composite indices (Ács et al., 2014). The framework establishes three theoretical properties — Recursive Scale Invariance, Capability-Knowledge Inheritance, and Ceiling Elevation — and introduces a formal distinction between Self-directed and State-mediated Ceiling Elevation with different implications for Coherence sustainability and transferability. The paper demonstrates analytical robustness through four comparative case studies spanning Digital, FinTech, BioTech, and organizational innovation ecosystems across eight national and organizational contexts. Seven theoretical contributions are identified: a two-axis quadrant taxonomy with Frascati Manual grounding; a formally specified causal ECM; a nine-cell taxonomy; a twelve-dimension scoring instrument; Recursive Scale Invariance and Capability-Knowledge Inheritance as named theoretical properties; Ceiling Elevation as a named strategic mechanism; and a statistically grounded ECM scoring methodology with Leontief non-compensability as its formal foundation.

detail.abstract:
This paper proposes the Autonomous Institutional Trust Standard (AITS) — a constitutional standard for autonomous digital finance and tokenised financial environments. AITS specifies the requirements any trust verification architecture must satisfy as a matter of constitutional necessity. It is not a system, a protocol, or a platform. It is an open constitutional specification that any institution in any jurisdiction may implement using its own technology, provided the constitutional core is satisfied.

The constitutional architecture operates at four levels, derived through deductive constitutional reasoning from foundational principles. Five Foundational Pillars ground the standard in real economic activity: (I) Legality; (II) Reexchangeable Value Generation — which constitutionally grounds anti-money laundering, because instruments whose underlying activity does not re-enter the legitimate economy fail at the pillar level before AML compliance is considered; (III) Human Consumability; (IV) Ownership-Based Transferability; and (V) Legal Enforceability and Verifiability. Eight Core Elements specify the operational requirements the pillars generate: (I) Transparency; (II) Explainability; (III) Auditability; (IV) Physical Substance; (V) Legality; (VI) Entitled Ownership; (VII) Transferability; and (VIII) Human Consumability. Seven Independence Principles govern how the standard operates and protects itself from capture: (I) Source Independence; (II) Graded Admissibility; (III) Decomposability; (IV) Tool and Methodology Neutrality; (V) Jurisdictional Neutrality; (VI) Symmetric Accountability; and (VII) Institutional Non-Capture. Ten Implementation Conditions declare what any compliant implementation must produce in technology-neutral terms: (I) Autonomous; (II) Continuous; (III) Real-time; (IV) Identifiable; (V) Executable; (VI) Measurable; (VII) Reportable; (VIII) Remote Accessible; (IX) Recordable; and (X) Storable. The Trust Redline is the supreme constitutional provision: any provision, practice, or change that reduces verifiability or weakens any pillar, element, or principle is discarded regardless of justification.

Subject matter jurisdiction covers nine admissible instrument categories spanning physical assets, operating businesses, licensed service operations, trade finance instruments across seven sub-categories, physical construction finance, revenue participations, contingent obligations, structured pools, and digital transformation pathways — assessed against six admissibility criteria and declared across seven financial domains. Two inadmissible categories exclude instruments that fail constitutively: those with no physical or licensed grounding, and those that cannot be independently audited. Both fail Pillar (II) at the constitutional level because their underlying activity does not generate value that circulates within the legitimate economy.

title: AI and Workforce Transformation: From Job Replacement to Job Redesign

detail.title: AI and Workforce Transformation: From Job Replacement to Job Redesign
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is transforming the workforce by changing tasks, roles, skills, and organizational workflows. While much attention is given to the fear of job replacement, this article argues that the deeper impact of AI lies in job redesign. AI can automate routine and repetitive activities, but it can also augment human capabilities by supporting analysis, communication, creativity, forecasting, decision-making, and productivity. As a result, many jobs are likely to be restructured rather than fully eliminated. The article discusses how AI affects work at the task level, highlights the importance of human-AI collaboration, and identifies emerging skills such as AI literacy, data literacy, critical thinking, adaptability, ethical awareness, and lifelong learning. It also examines organizational readiness, responsible AI governance, reskilling, and risks such as bias, inequality, employee anxiety, and overdependence on AI. The article concludes that AI should be managed as a strategic opportunity to redesign work while preserving human value.

title: Vocational Atrophy in the age of AI and the Case for Logotherapy

detail.title: Vocational Atrophy in the age of AI and the Case for Logotherapy
detail.abstract: The psychological literature on the impact of artificial intelligence on work culture has concentrated on the threat of job displacement, that is, the prospect that automation will eliminate roles and leave workers without employment. This paper introduces a different framing on how AI would impact employment in the future. This paper argues that the immediate threat is not the elimination of work but that it is being stripped of substance. The progressive absorption by AI systems of the cognitively demanding and technically challenging aspects of professional tasks is leaving behind work that is nominally present but psychologically diminished. This paper introduces the concept of vocational atrophy to describe this condition, the withering of professional meaning not through job loss but through the erosion of what made the work worth doing. Taking inspiration from Frankl's logotherapy, Csikszentmihalyi's flow theory, Jahoda's latent deprivation model, and selfdetermination theory, the paper maps the psychological mechanisms through which AI erodes work-based meaning. It supports this argument with real institutional evidence, including high-profile legal sanctions, regulatory failures, and costly fraud losses, that demonstrates cognitive atrophy already manifesting in elite professional settings. The paper further argues that the technological singularity adds a future existential threat. As a direct response to these pressures, logotherapy, which focuses on the will to meaning, is proposed as the most appropriate clinical and conceptual framework to deal with the existential vacuum caused by the loss of work based meaning. The paper develops theoretical and organizational implications, and suggests a research agenda for a phenomenon that is already underway but has yet to receive adequate attention.

title: Hungry Monster: Professional Recognition Hunger and the Emotional Metabolism of Abusive Leadership
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Hungry Monster: Professional Recognition Hunger and the Emotional Metabolism of Abusive Leadership
detail.abstract:
This paper theorizes abusive leadership and power-harassment-like managerial behavior not merely as anger expression, personality pathology, or failure of emotion regulation, but as an emotional metabolism driven by professional recognition hunger. It introduces the concept of the Hungry Monster, defined as a leadership condition in which a manager, driven by hunger for professional recognition, managerial legitimacy, competence, and indispensability, temporarily satisfies that hunger through subordinates’ submission, silence, intimidation, dependence, and inability to object.

The paper builds on and integrates prior theoretical models, including the theory of untouchable symbols, the Angry Monster model, the Anger LEAK Model, and the Meme Breaker framework. Whereas the Angry Monster model explains how abusive supervisory behavior becomes difficult to correct through upward feedback blockage, symbolic protection, and mimetic reproduction of anger, the Hungry Monster model addresses a deeper question: why does such a manager need anger, control, submission, and justification so intensely?

The central argument is that the Angry Monster is often also a Hungry Monster. Anger is the visible surface; beneath it lies professional recognition hunger—the desire to be recognized as competent, legitimate, indispensable, and necessary to the workplace. When this hunger is satisfied not through mutual recognition, employee growth, or organizational learning, but through subordinates’ silence, submission, fear, and dependence, leadership shifts from development to consumption.

The paper proposes the Hungry Monster Loop. Professional recognition hunger generates sensitivity to threats against the managerial self-image. Subordinates’ mistakes, objections, autonomy, or alternative proposals are perceived as threats. Anger, intimidation, public correction, excessive control, and labeling are then activated. Subordinates become silent, compliant, and psychologically diminished. This silence is misrecognized as approval, legitimacy, or successful control. Temporary emotional satiety is achieved, yet the underlying hunger remains unresolved, leading to renewed anger and control.

The paper also distinguishes between the broad and narrow meanings of the Hungry Monster. Broadly, the concept may apply to other recognition-driven environments, including visibility economies, moral outrage, and attention-seeking risk escalation. More narrowly, this paper focuses on workplace-based Hungry Monsters: leaders who feed on subordinates’ silence and submission as professional recognition resources.

Finally, the paper argues that preventing Hungry Monsters requires more than anger management or individual warning. Organizations must redesign the flow of recognition by institutionalizing upward feedback, limiting symbolic protection, monitoring label-framing practices, distinguishing the functionality of anger from its necessity, and evaluating managers not only by short-term outcomes but by what those outcomes consume. The key question is not simply whether a manager produces results, but what is being eaten to produce them.

detail.abstract:
The rapid deployment of embodied AI — humanoid robots capable of performing physical labor across manufacturing, agriculture, logistics, and construction — threatens to concentrate the productivity gains of the coming industrial revolution among a narrow class of capital owners, replicating and accelerating the distributional failures of prior technological transitions. This paper proposes the Labor Copy Model, a propertyrightsbased institutional framework that ensures universal participation in the robot economy through productive asset ownership rather than transfer payments.

The model assigns each citizen one laborsubstitution robot whose income accrues directly to its owner. Four parallel distribution channels — market purchase, government targeted credit, free distribution, and mandatory displacement compensation — guarantee access regardless of prior wealth. An automation displacement tax creates a selfbalancing feedback loop: the more firms automate, the more capital flows to those most affected.

The paper develops the complete case for viability across three dimensions:

(1) economic mechanisms, including price trajectories, wagefloor derivation, and quotatax feedback loops; 

(2) social conditions, including education reconstruction, psychological stability, and cohesion mechanisms; and 

(3) political feasibility, demonstrating that the model generates no rational opposition coalition.

The framework is situated in dialogue with Acemoglu and Restrepo’s taskdisplacement model, Marinescu’s dual safetynet architecture, Nayebi’s productivitythreshold analysis, and the UBI tradition — arguing that predistribution via universal robot ownership is a more durable institutional response to automationdriven inequality than redistribution.

A phased global diffusion strategy addresses developed, developing, and least developed economies. Limitations — including quantitative parameter uncertainty, softwareAI displacement, geopolitical constraints, and crossborder capital risks — are explicitly acknowledged. The framework’s empirical grounding is reinforced by a continuous stream of realworld developments — from judicial rulings on AIdriven dismissal to government robotidentity registration pilots to commercial humanoid deployments breaking operational records — each an independent confirmation that the transition described in this paper is already underway.

The paper concludes by positioning the Labor Copy Model as an open institutional platform for economists, legal scholars, and policymakers to refine.

Central thesis: design the institution well enough, and human nature needs no improvement.

detail.abstract: The disruptive potential of AI-enabled applications for competitive dynamics and the core organisational forms of digital intermediation inevitably also has significant implications for the recent regulatory initiatives adopted to govern digital markets. Indeed, because these instruments were conceived without AI specifically in view, they risk becoming outdated within a very short period of time. Notably, while they have been shaped by a Big Tech-centred conception of digital markets, the possible emergence of new gatekeepers in the age of AI marks a turning point that calls into question the very rationale and foundations of these regimes in their present form. As a result, only a few years after its enactment, the role of the DMA, together with its rationale and claimed future-proof character, is already under scrutiny, as the deployment of AI applications raises the question whether policymakers should reopen the legislative framework in order to amend the Regulation. Against this background and in the context of the first review of the DMA, the paper argues that the rise of AI applications calls for a reconsideration of the DMA's overall architecture and for the development of a distinct competition policy framework, rather than for a merely incremental fine-tuning exercise.

detail.abstract: This study investigates the effect of organizational culture on employee performance within the technology sector, using a leading Egyptian IT solutions company as the empirical context. Organizational culture is conceptualized through Denison's (1990) four-dimensional model (Involvement, Consistency, Adaptability, and Mission), while employee performance is measured using Koopmans et al.'s (2014) Individual Work Performance (IWP) model, covering task performance, contextual performance, and counterproductive work behavior. A mixedmethod design was employed: quantitative data were collected from 301 employees via a structured questionnaire, while qualitative depth was obtained through semi-structured openended interviews analyzed using Schein's (1985) Three-Level Model. Findings reveal a strong, statistically significant positive relationship between organizational culture and employee performance (R² = 0.543, rs = .739, p < .001). Mission emerged as the strongest predictor (β = .291), followed by Adaptability (β = .244) and Consistency (β = .258). Contextual performance showed the strongest cultural association (rs = .659), surpassing task performance. Qualitative analysis identified collaboration, quality commitment, and open communication as deeply embedded cultural assumptions driving performance. The study contributes empirical evidence from the Egyptian technology sector and offers actionable recommendations for culture-based performance management.

title: Admissibility and the Feasibility of Exchange

detail.title: Admissibility and the Feasibility of Exchange
detail.abstract: Economic activity often requires actors to undertake actions that expose them to potential loss prior to the realization of returns. This paper develops a framework in which such actions are governed by an admissibility condition: exchange is feasible only when the unrecoverable portion of potential loss remains within an actor's continuation capacity. By emphasizing admissibility, the analysis identifies a feasibility boundary that precedes optimization. While much of the existing literature focuses on how exchange is structured in the presence of frictions, the framework highlights whether exchange can occur at all. When this condition fails, no contract, price, or incentive structure can sustain the interaction ex post. Allowing recovery to vary across counterparties introduces relational heterogeneity into this feasibility condition. The same action may be feasible with some counterparties and infeasible with others, generating domain-bounded exchange. This mechanism produces exposuredependent segmentation: low-exposure activities remain broadly integrated, while high-exposure activities cluster within high-recovery domains defined by admissibility constraints. The framework also implies nonlinear responses to institutional change. Improvements in recovery may have limited effects on low-exposure exchange but can generate discrete expansions in high-exposure activity by shifting interactions from infeasible to feasible. In addition, admissibility induces structured interaction patterns, including assortative matching and clustering within high-recovery environments. Because continuation capacity and relational recovery are substitutes in the admissibility condition, the model generates asymmetry across actors: large actors can undertake highexposure actions in weaker institutional environments, while smaller actors remain constrained to strong-recovery domains. More broadly, the framework links feasibility constraints to segmentation, interaction structure, and economic fragility as joint outcomes of admissibility constraints.

detail.abstract:
Background: Section 3060 of the 21st Century Cures Act created a statutory carve-out, codified at 21 U.S.C. §360j(o)(1)(E), that excludes qualifying clinical decision support (CDS) functions from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) device definition. FDA's 2022 final guidance, revised in January 2026, defines the boundary of that carve-out but is silent on how a developer should run a quality system to remain inside it. The Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology (ONC, now ASTP/ONC) imposes intervention-risk-management duties under 45 C.F.R. §170.315(b)(11), but only on developers of certified health IT modules, leaving standalone Non-Device CDS vendors with no established quality regime.

Objective: To synthesize an adapted, vendor-side quality management system (QMS) reference model for Non-Device CDS.

Methods: We mapped ISO 9001:2015, ISO 13485:2016 design controls, ISO 14971:2019, IEC 62304, IEC 82304-1, ISPE GAMP 5, FDA Computer Software Assurance, and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework / ISO/IEC 42001 onto a single QMS spine, and grounded a hazard model in the four FDA exemption criteria. We instantiated the model in precision oncology using public knowledge sources (CIViC, CPIC, ClinVar, ClinicalTrials.gov) under the AMP/ASCO/CAP 2017 framework.

Results: We present four artifacts: (1) a clause-by-clause cross-walk from ISO 9001 §4–10 to Non-Device CDS obligations; (2) a four-family hazard taxonomy keyed to the statutory criteria; (3) a change-control SOP for clinically consequential, non-software knowledge content; and (4) a worked example with a populated risk-management file, a design-history-file table of contents, a supplier-qualification list, and a post-deployment surveillance plan. 

Conclusions: A non-device QMS, built on ISO 9001 rather than ISO 13485, can hold Non-Device CDS to clinical-grade quality without asserting device status. The framework is voluntary and does not substitute for FDA jurisdiction if a product crosses into device CDS.

detail.abstract:
This Briefing Paper examines the evolving procurement fraud enforcement landscape and identifies emerging risk areas that government contractors should monitor. While procurement fraud has long been an enforcement priority across administrations, the current Department of Justice has aggressively expanded its use of the False Claims Act (FCA) and related authorities, embedding fraud enforcement into the contractor compliance infrastructure through new task forces, mandatory contract clauses, Federal Acquisition Regulation deviations, and disclosure obligations aligned with current policy priorities including cybersecurity, anti-discrimination, and trade compliance.

The Paper begins by mapping the federal fraud enforcement taxonomy, distinguishing among criminal fraud provisions under Title 18, the civil False Claims Act, and the Administrative False Claims Act, with attention to how the Supreme Court's 2025 decision in Kousisis v. United States expanded prosecutorial reach by rejecting the economic loss requirement in fraudulent-inducement wire fraud cases.

The Paper then analyzes the expanding reach of certification-based liability under the FCA. Three developments are driving this expansion: the proliferation of certification requirements in substantive areas that did not previously carry them, the government's affirmative incorporation of materiality findings into contract clauses, and the shift toward fixed-price and commercial-type contracting that reduces traditional cost-accounting oversight. The Paper examines how Escobar's materiality framework now anchors both civil FCA and criminal wire fraud analysis post-Kousisis.

The Paper identifies four substantive areas where this enforcement model is being deployed: cybersecurity, where DOJ's Civil Cyber-Fraud Initiative has produced significant civil settlements and a recent criminal indictment; anti-discrimination compliance, where Executive Order 14398 and FAR 52.222-90 build FCA materiality language directly into contracts; trade compliance, where the new DOJ Trade Fraud Task Force has driven settlements including the $54.4 million Ceratizit USA resolution; and AI compliance, which presents both nascent regulatory risk through GSA's draft AI clause and immediate fraud-facilitation risk through cases involving AI-generated fraudulent records.

The Paper then examines the qui tam environment, including DOJ's April 2026 launch of the Fraud Oversight through Careful Use of Statistics (FOCUS) initiative formalizing the relationship with data-miner relators, the constitutional challenge to qui tam practice in United States ex rel. Zafirov v. Florida Medical Associates, and the practical considerations contractors face when potential misconduct surfaces, including the tension between FAR mandatory disclosure requirements and DOJ's new Department-wide Corporate Enforcement Policy. The Paper concludes with fourteen practical guidelines for managing exposure in this evolving environment.

detail.title: Understanding the Diversification-Firm Value Nexus in Mining Firms Listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange: A Systematic Review and Conceptual Framework

detail.abstract: This study examines the relationship between business diversification and firm value in mining companies listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange through a systematic literature review (SLR) approach. The existing literature presents inconsistent findings regarding whether diversification enhances or reduces firm value, highlighting the need for a more comprehensive and integrative understanding of this relationship, particularly within resource-based industries. Using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) framework, this study analyzes 33 peerreviewed articles published between 2021 and 2025. The findings indicate that diversification does not exert a direct and uniform effect on firm value. Instead, its impact is mediated by key internal mechanisms, including financial performance, capital structure, risk management, and internal capital markets. Furthermore, the effectiveness of diversification strategies is shaped by moderating factors such as firm size, corporate governance, commodity price dynamics, and macroeconomic conditions. The results reveal that related diversification tends to enhance firm value through synergy and efficient resource utilization, whereas unrelated diversification may lead to value destruction due to agency problems and increased organizational complexity. These findings underscore the non-linear and context-dependent nature of the diversification-firm value relationship, particularly in the mining sector, which is characterized by high volatility and capital intensity. This study contributes to the literature by developing an integrative conceptual framework that bridges strategic management and corporate finance perspectives. The framework provides a comprehensive explanation of how diversification influences firm value through interconnected mediating and moderating mechanisms. The findings also offer practical implications for managers of mining companies listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange in designing effective diversification strategies aligned with firm capabilities and external conditions.

title: Artificial Intelligence And Dynamic Capability Development In Emerging Market SMES: A Strategic Management Perspective

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence And Dynamic Capability Development In Emerging Market SMES: A Strategic Management Perspective
detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) has become an increasingly important strategic technology for firms seeking to improve decision-making, adaptability, and competitive renewal. However, the relationship between AI adoption and dynamic capability development remains insufficiently explained, particularly in small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) operating in emerging markets. These firms often face institutional instability, resource constraints, limited digital infrastructure, and uneven access to advanced technological expertise. As a result, existing AI adoption research, which has largely emphasized technological implementation and operational efficiency, provides only a partial explanation of how AI contributes to strategic adaptation in such contexts.

This study develops an integrative theoretical framework explaining how AI adoption contributes to dynamic capability formation in emerging market SMEs. Drawing on the dynamic capabilities perspective and the resource-based view of the firm, the paper conceptualizes AI not simply as a technological asset, but as a strategic enabler that may strengthen firms’ sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring capabilities under conditions of uncertainty.

The study is based on a systematic literature review conducted in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 protocol. Eighty-seven peer-reviewed studies published between 2019 and 2024 were identified and analyzed through thematic analysis and narrative synthesis. The review included studies indexed in Web of Science, Scopus, EBSCOhost Business Source Complete, and Google Scholar in order to capture relevant contributions across strategic management, digital transformation, SME, and emerging market research.

The findings suggest that AI adoption in emerging market SMEs is often reactive and shaped by competitive pressure, survival needs, and institutional constraints rather than by deliberate long-term capability-building strategies. The analysis identifies absorptive capacity as a central mechanism through which AI-related knowledge is converted into organizational learning, strategic adaptation, and capability renewal. It also shows that institutional voids, including inadequate digital infrastructure, regulatory uncertainty, limited access to advanced expertise, and fragmented innovation ecosystems, substantially shape the relationship between AI adoption and dynamic capability development.

In response to these findings, the study proposes the AI-Enabled Dynamic Capability (AEDC) Framework, a context-sensitive conceptual model that integrates AI adoption, dynamic capabilities, absorptive capacity, and emerging market institutional conditions. The framework contributes to strategic management and international business research by explaining how resource-constrained SMEs may develop competitive resilience through AI-enabled organizational transformation. The study also offers practical implications for SME managers, policymakers, and development institutions seeking to design more effective AI adoption and digital capability-building strategies in emerging economies.

detail.abstract: De minimis (Latin for "about minimal things") refers to a customs exemption that allowed imports valued below $800 to enter the United States duty-free and with simplified border processing. As cross-border e-commerce expanded, this administrative rule became politically contested, especially amid concerns about large direct-from-abroad platforms and competitive pressure from foreign sellers. We study what happens when this channel is removed in a different but economically important setting: a marketplace where foreign and domestic sellers compete side by side, and where the exposed foreign sellers are largely outside the Chinacentered supply chains that dominated the policy debate. Using seller-week data from Etsy around the 2025 suspension of duty-free de minimis exemption, we estimate how the policy affected cross-border marketplace trade in one of Etsy's largest categories. Non-U.S. sellers lose sales after the policy change, with weekly unit sales falling by about 18% after implementation and remaining similarly depressed more than six months later. Some demand shifts toward U.S. sellers, especially smaller shops, but these gains are too small in volume terms to offset the losses among foreign sellers. The losses are concentrated among larger non-U.S. sellers, while the gains accrue mainly to smaller U.S. shops, so total category activity falls. The results show that removing a duty-free channel can reduce competitive pressure from foreign sellers, but it can also eliminate cross-border transactions that are not fully replaced on the domestic side of the marketplace.

detail.abstract: We study how a large foreign direct investment (FDI) project affects household labor supply decisions, sectoral labor allocation, and gender-specific outcomes in a developing country. Exploiting the entry of a large export-oriented electronics manufacturing investment in Vietnam in 2008, we use a difference-indifferences design and data from the Vietnamese Household Living Standards Survey (2004-2020) to compare labor market outcomes in provinces exposed to the investment to those in unexposed provinces. We find that the investment led to a substantial reallocation of labor from informal employment and agriculture into formal wage work, with no significant change in overall labor supply or total hours worked. Formal-sector hours and earnings increase sharply, while informal-sector hours decline and informal earnings remain largely unchanged, resulting in higher total wage income. These effects are overwhelmingly driven by women aged 18-35, consistent with the gender composition of labor demand associated with the investment examined in this paper. We also find evidence of modest increases in educational attainment, particularly among young women. Overall, the results show that large-scale FDI can induce meaningful structural change in local labor markets and generate gender-differentiated gains through sectoral labor reallocation. detail.title: Deep Flow Networks
detail.abstract: We introduce Deep Flow Networks (DFNs), a new class of discrete function approximators. DFNs are inspired by and generalize minimum-cost flow value functions that map node imbalances on a subset of nodes to the optimal flow cost. Such functions are known to be M-convex Murota (2003) and admit efficient optimization. On the theoretical side, we prove that DFNs are universal approximators for discrete functions on Z d that admit convex extensions to R d , and characterize their optimization complexity in terms of their deviation from the M-convex regime. Guided by these results, we develop a practical DFN implementation for learning from data. Finally, we evaluate our implementation empirically on data from different ground-truth functions, showing that DFNs achieve strong approximation accuracy while being substantially faster to optimize than benchmark approaches.

detail.title: Value Creation Thinking in M&A: The Importance of Counterfactual Thinking
detail.abstract: This working paper presents recent research in M&A that counters the prevailing wisdom that companies engaged in M&As often destroy value. Excessive bidder prices for target companies are presented as evidence of this conclusion. This working paper points out that this thinking is faulty and that the logic regarding the value creation or destruction of M&A activities needs to be revised. It presents counterfactual thinking as the basis for accurate value creation thinking and it also underlines the role of obsolescence as a trigger for M&A initiatives. The research further generates a number of conclusions that go against prevailing wisdom in the M&A area. For one, markets are more efficient than commonly perceived. Second, value destruction has two facets, and not just one. Value destruction is not only the consequence of excessive M&A prices or faulty integrations, but should also consider the opportunity costs associated with missed value creating opportunities. Third, in a context of major technological and economic disruption (as triggered by digitalization or the current COVID-19 pandemic), one might expect higher value bids and a greater number to be fully consistent with economic rationality. Fourth, well governed boards must understand that counterfactual thinking allows them to set upper limits to the size of value creating acquisition bids. Finally, counterfactual thinking is also the thinking that ought to drive board decision marking in related settings such as CEO inventives and succession planning, areas known to be responsible for regular value destruction.

detail.abstract:
AI Displacement Sovereign Risk™ (ADSR™) is a sovereign stress-testing framework for the fiscal volatility generated when AI-driven human capital displacement proceeds faster than a sovereign's fiscal, insurance, pension and labour-market systems can absorb the transition. ADSR™ is explicitly not a forecast of mass unemployment. Consistent with the 2026 state of the art (Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta; BIS Working Paper 1325; IMF SDN/2026/001), it accepts that aggregate employment may remain stable while displacement is asymmetric and concentrated, and it measures the resulting transition friction and contingent fiscal liability, not the level of joblessness.

The framework introduces a four-dimension sovereign risk matrix calibrated against the AI Sovereign Liability Index™ (ASLI™) benchmark, specifying trigger thresholds, GDP-impact ranges and pre-defined policy instruments deployable within existing institutional mandates. It completes the architecture HSAS™ → CDP™ → ASLI™ → HCB™ → EDD™ → ADSR™. Version 2 adds a Transition Friction Model reframing the contribution as transition-volatility stress-testing; a velocity sensitivity table; a Productivity–Employment Wedge reconciling ADSR™ with stable-employment evidence; a Contingent Liability Accounting treatment; a Policy Timing Risk analysis; and a Governance Architecture specifying who calculates, verifies, publishes and audits the index. detail.title: How America’s Governance Went from Great to Bad: An Essay on the Erosion of the Governance Genius that Created America
detail.abstract: This essay tries to demonstrate how America's governance system, long regarded as an example for democracies to follow around the world, radically changed in nature through the introduction of legislation that allowed the abolishment through Citizens United vs FEC Supreme Court ruling of 2010 that abolished limits on donations from individuals, corporations, and labor unions to Political Action Committees (PACs). It then argues how this democratic loophole, in conjunction with a second one that allows unlimited terms for elected officials, has turned the elected body of officials into a gerontocracy that has become entrenched in its own survival, and unresponsive to the people these officials are meant to represent. Furthermore, and even more fatal, is that the combined effects of these two loopholes has blocked the Amendment System that the framers of the Constitution designed, being aware that the Constitution they had framed was imperfect and needed to be regularly reviewed and updated in order to build the "ever perfect Union" these founders envisioned. One immediate conclusion is that the current US electoral process is no longer the means for "We, the People" to sanction politicians that do not contribute to build this Union, do not seek to establish Justice, nor insure domestic Tranquility, nor promote the general Welfare or secure the blessings of Liberty. It shows how any governance system, no matter how good in appearance or public opinion, is unavoidably imperfect, remains work in progress, and how it can become corrupted by apparently simple rule changes whose far flung effect are hard to fathom the day they are approved. Finally, it is intended as a reminder of the vital necessity of any governance system to be regularly reviewed for the extent it continues to foster the goals it was established to serve and promote.

detail.abstract:
Search engine optimization has traditionally treated the ranked web page as the main unit of work and rank position as the main visibility proxy. AI-mediated discovery weakens that model. Generative search systems, answer engines, large language models, and browser agents can retrieve passages, issue derived queries, synthesize answers, attach citations, and recommend entities without presenting a stable ranked list of pages. This working paper introduces SEEN, a four-layer framework for Generative Engine Optimization: Structure, Evidence, Entity, and Notability. SEEN reframes optimization around an entity's evidence corpus rather than a single owned page. It asks whether an entity is easy for AI systems to find, read, verify, resolve, and recommend.

The paper synthesizes platform documentation, academic work on generative engine optimization and conversational SEO, empirical studies of Google AI Overviews, retrieval-augmented generation mechanisms, evidence-evaluation research, knowledge-graph grounding, crawler documentation, and industry studies of AI search citations. It contributes: (1) a stage-aware model of AI visibility; (2) a four-layer entity-corpus framework; (3) a 41-item practitioner checklist that operationalizes the framework; and (4) a conservative validation agenda for future empirical work. The paper does not claim that SEEN guarantees citations, recommendations, rankings, or traffic. Instead, it argues that AI visibility should be analyzed as a corpus-engineering problem in which owned content, platform-hosted first-party content, and third-party corroboration must read as one coherent, verifiable entity.

detail.abstract: This extensive academic thesis examines the phenomenon of food waste at national and European levels, analyzing the deeper organizational, institutional, and economic causes that trigger it across all individual stages of the modern supply chain. The objective of this study is the analytical presentation and thorough description of a proposed, strictly for-profit digital application and two-sided marketplace platform (B2B and B2C), which utilizes state-of-theart information technologies to bridge the existing gap between the supply and demand of surplus food in the Greek market. title: The Autonomy-Control Paradox: How Enterprise Business Intelligence Democratization Alters Decision Rights in Corporate Hierarchies

detail.title: The Autonomy-Control Paradox: How Enterprise Business Intelligence Democratization Alters Decision Rights in Corporate Hierarchies
detail.abstract:
The promise of data democratization, defined as the widespread distribution of analytical tools across a corporate hierarchy has become a cornerstone of modern digital transformation strategies (Vial, 2019). In the pharmaceutical sector, where firms manage vast portfolios across complex distribution channels, the shift from centralized reporting to interactive business intelligence (BI) and AI-enabled CRM ecosystems was intended to foster data-driven cultures and empower localized decision making. 

However, drawing on 15 years of practitioner experience, this paper identifies a contradictory outcome: as BI systems become more pervasive, corporate headquarters acquire unprecedented visibility into frontline actions, triggering a recentralization of organizational control. 

We term this the autonomy-control paradox - a structural condition in which managers are nominally empowered yet simultaneously subjected to granular algorithmic oversight that restricts professional discretion. Drawing on organizational economics (Jensen & Meckling, 1992), Foucauldian surveillance theory (Foucault, 1977), institutional decoupling (Meyer & Rowan, 1977), and sociomaterial agency (Leonardi & Barley, 2010; Orlikowski, 2000), we introduce the concept of Algorithmic Enclosure to describe the structural state in which centralized BI systems so dominate operations that independent managerial discretion is marginalized. 

We identify two operational flashpoints - automated targeting versus field agency and data panopticism versus localized sensemaking and introduce Information System Deviance to describe the workaround behaviors frontline staff adopt to navigate these tensions. Six testable propositions are derived, a governance typology is proposed, and a multi-method empirical roadmap is outlined. The paper contributes to IS research by naming a paradox practitioners experience, but scholars have not yet systematically conceptualized, and by demonstrating how the paradox generates path-dependent dynamics that resist conventional governance solutions.

detail.abstract:
Background: Leaders have called to improve healthcare professionals’ capacity as agents of change. This study tested the idea of comprehensively redesigning clinical training, in collaboration with students, to promote patient-centred healthcare.

Methods: This study transformed the first clinical year of undergraduate medical education at Witten/Herdecke University into a longitudinal integrated clerkship (LIC), in which students achieve their main learning objectives by accompanying patients through the healthcare system. The authors employed a participatory action research approach and describe the implementation process through analyses of team meeting minutes, stakeholder interviews, and additional documents, including field observations.

Findings: The study lasted 29 months and consisted of four phases (I–IV). Students participated in this collaborative inquiry in multiple ways, including serving in the core team (I–IV), participating in a student initiative (II–IV), and piloting the LIC prototype (III and IV). After exploring the opportunities, challenges, and critical elements of an LIC, the core team launched a symposium involving students, professors, healthcare teams, and international experts to discuss the potential of students as co-providers in healthcare. A subsequent student initiative created an LIC prototype, which was ultimately accepted by institutional faculty, with 11 students applying to participate in the pilot. Upon completion of the LIC pilot, surveys of students, preceptors, and patients indicated that the students successfully established longitudinal relationships with patients, providing them with critical support. The students bridged outpatient and inpatient services and initiated a patient-centred community of local healthcare providers with university experts.

Interpretation: This study defined and involved students as co-creators of change who both ideated and implemented comprehensive educational innovations. Students’ change agency may be supported by empowering them to play autonomous roles in education and healthcare.

detail.title: Do People Support Information Campaigns About Inequality?
detail.abstract: We study beliefs about whether information campaigns can shift public support for redistribution in a survey with more than 3,000 respondents. We randomly provide respondents with evidence from a meta-study about the share of information interventions that do not significantly affect redistributive preferences. This information strongly changes respondents’ beliefs about the effectiveness of such campaigns. Descriptively, respondents who are more skeptical about the effectiveness of information campaigns are also less supportive of disseminating such information. However, we find no causal effect of experimentally shifting these beliefs on support for government provision of inequality-related information to the public, which is generally high. We analyze open-ended responses to study why experimentally shifting beliefs about the effectiveness of information campaigns does not affect support for information dissemination.

detail.abstract: Using a structural VAR with a relatively agnostic identification based on narrative sign restrictions, this paper, in line with recent empirical evidence, documents an increase in the labor share following restrictive monetary policy in the euro area. We then complement the empirical analysis with a theoretical investigation that provides mechanisms linking monetary policy and the labor share — a connection that has so far been regarded as lacking an explanation. Specifically, we show that the observed responses of the labor share, real wages, and productivity to a monetary policy shock can be reconciled within an otherwise standard New Keynesian framework once capital accumulation is introduced and both nominal and real frictions — in particular, labor adjustment costs — are incorporated.

detail.abstract:
The term “deep-tech innovation” has attracted growing attention in research, policy, and practice, but it is applied inconsistently and lacks an agreed-upon definition. This limits cumulative knowledge building and blurs how deep-tech innovation relates to adjacent concepts. We address this gap by developing a framework that treats deep-tech innovation as a distinct object of inquiry. Using a multi-method design that combines a systematic, integrative, concept-centric literature review and semi-structured interviews with deep-tech founders, we identify twelve defining attributes structured across three levels: invention, venture, and ecosystem. At the invention level (the conceptual core), we specify six attributes: three foundational attributes that capture the scientific and technological basis of the invention, and three attributes that describe its characteristic exposure profile. The remaining six attributes capture recurring implications at the venture level (staged financing strategies, dual scientific and commercial maturation, and the multidisciplinary broadening of teams) and the ecosystem level (multi-actor interactions, specialized incubation support, and industrial de-risking and scaling partnerships). We use this framework to delineate the boundaries of deep-tech innovation, distinguish it from adjacent concepts, and propose an agenda for future research.

title: A Bayesian Critic for Frequentist Procedures
affiliations: Harvard Society of Fellows, Harvard University and Harvard University - Department of Economics

detail.title: A Bayesian Critic for Frequentist Procedures
detail.abstract:
We propose a method for automated, probabilistic evaluation of the frequentist properties (e.g., bias, coverage) of procedures (e.g., estimators, confidence intervals) in a given setting. A Bayesian critic observes a sample of data and updates their prior belief on the underlying data-generating process (DGP). The resulting posterior belief about the DGP implies a posterior belief about the property of interest. When the critic's prior is in a low-precision Dirichlet process class, the critic's posterior can be approximated via a Bayesian bootstrap, making the method fully automated. We apply the method to several canonical settings and show that the critic shares some concerns raised in previous work and delivers new insights.

title: Off the Labor Supply Curve: The Zero Employer Size Wage Effect Within Large Firms
affiliations: Halle Institute for Economic Research, Centre for European Economic Research (ZEW), University of Erlangen-Nuremberg-Friedrich Alexander Universität Erlangen Nürnberg and University of California, Berkeley

detail.title: Off the Labor Supply Curve: The Zero Employer Size Wage Effect Within Large Firms
detail.abstract:
We revisit the employer size wage effect (ESWE)—arguably the most basic and influential departure from the law of one price for labor. Our main result is that this canonical fact disappears completely across establishments within the same firm, even though they operate in different local labor markets. We uncover and dissect this fact by including a firm fixed effect in otherwise standard cross-sectional regressions of wages on establishment size. We implement this demanding specification in population-wide triple-linked firm-establishment-employee data in Germany. This result is new in the ESWE literature (for which our paper also provides the first systematic meta-analysis). This wage-size decoupling is hard to square with the view that employment is determined along a finitely elastic employer-specific labor supply curve—i.e., employers pay exactly the minimum needed for the quantity of labor, but no more—the foundation of the monopsony view. By contrast, large multi-establishment firms (MEF) appear to hire off their labor supply curves (or those curves are very elastic), pay wage premia above the monopsonistic minimum, and leave excess labor supply. We find some evidence for a reemergence of the ESWE within low-premium MEFs. Overall, at least for the 25% of German employment in large firms for which the ESWE disappears, wage setting and employment determination may be better accounted for by alternative models, namely accommodating above-market-clearing wage premia and rationing of labor supply, such as efficiency wage theories.

title: Growing Together and Apart: Scale Economies and Labor Specialization in Global Value Chains
affiliations: , University of Copenhagen, BI Norwegian Business School,  and Purdue University

detail.title: Growing Together and Apart: Scale Economies and Labor Specialization in Global Value Chains
detail.abstract: We study how firm growth reorganizes the division of labor across firms in global value chains. Using a novel dataset linking cross-border firm-to-firm transactions to matched employer–employee data, we show that demand shocks increase trade between firms while reducing occupational similarity, implying greater specialization. We develop and estimate a model of task outsourcing in which firms expand by reallocating tasks to suppliers. The model matches the data and implies endogenous scale economies. Eliminating outsourcing reduces average labor productivity by 25 percent and increases input costs by 10 percent, highlighting the central role of specialization in shaping firm performance.
